visits.text: "La Suiza de México": the nickname seems exaggerated until you arrive in Arteaga. Nestled in the Sierra Madre Oriental, this Pueblo Mágico is surrounded by pine forests, flowering apple trees, and peaks that get snow in winter. The Templo de San Isidro Labrador, built in the 18th century, marks the town center and serves as the starting point for all walks.

The scent of apple blossoms dominates the entire Sierra de Arteaga from April to May. The apple orchards stretch as far as the eye can see from the road, interspersed with waterfalls and rivers. A sierra resort even offers skiing on artificial snow in summer—strange and perfectly Mexican.

activities.text: Buy a jar of apple preserves or a licor de durazno before leaving. The shops on Guerrero and Democracia streets specialize in these local products. La Quinta Fantasía is the reference dulcería: its dulces de durazno and perón are the object of a real regional cult.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeast Mexico: Monterrey, Desert & Mapimí, 14 days

visits.text: On a clear day, you can see the Popocatépetl volcano from Cerro de San Miguel, the hill in Atlixco. In November 2026, it is under a Yellow Alert, Phase 2, the intermediate level of Mexico’s volcanic alert system: authorities ask people to stay at least 12 km from the crater. It can therefore be admired from a distance. The climb begins at the Escalera Ancha, a broad staircase, and leads to the Capilla de San Miguel Arcángel, a 16th-century chapel. Admission is free; come early, as the morning mist lifts.

Atlixco’s Palacio Municipal houses murals by artist Juan Manuel Martínez Caltenco. The city has been designated a Pueblo Mágico since 2015. Before leaving, also take a look at the facade of the Capilla de la Tercera Orden, one of the city’s chapels.

activities.text: “Atlixco de las Flores” is the city’s nickname, and the viveros, or plant nurseries, in the Cabrera neighborhood explain why. Hundreds of growers cultivate plants and fruit trees here, in greenhouses and open fields. Toward the end of the year, the Nochebuena, or poinsettia, fair showcases about 25,000 plants in 27 varieties. Admission is free, from 8:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on weekdays and from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekends; bring cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Teotihuacán, Real del Monte, Tlaxcala, and Puebla in 7 Days

visits.text: Plundered by pirates in the 17th century, Bacalar protected itself with the Fuerte de San Felipe, completed in 1729. English, French, and Dutch pirates came for logwood, a tree used to produce dye. Today, the fort houses a museum of piracy and the Caste War, with weapons, maps, and model ships. Climb onto the ramparts for the best free view of the lagoon. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday.

Turquoise near the shores and dark blue above the sinkholes, Bacalar Lagoon owes its nickname, the Lagoon of Seven Colors, to variations in depth and light. It stretches for about forty kilometers. The Maya called the place Bakhalal, “the place of reeds.” The Spanish founded Salamanca de Bacalar here in 1545. Since 2006, the town has held Mexico’s Pueblo Mágico tourism designation. View the lagoon at sunrise or sunset, when its colors are at their best.

You’ll swim above more than 90 m of water at Cenote Azul, a few minutes south of Bacalar beside Highway 307. This open natural sinkhole is not connected to the lagoon. A restaurant sits at the water’s edge. Admission must be paid in cash. A life jacket is mandatory if you are not a strong swimmer, and sunscreen, lotions, and insect repellent are prohibited. Come early, before the groups, then continue toward Kohunlich.

activities.text: You’ll board at 8 a.m. for about three hours on Bacalar Lagoon, when the water is calm and there are few boats. The boat passes near the stromatolites, rocks formed very slowly by colonies of bacteria. It then crosses over Cenote Negro, a sinkhole about 70 m deep in the middle of the lagoon. It stops at Canal de los Piratas, also called Estero de Chac, which connects the lagoon to the Río Hondo, then follows the shore of Isla de los Pájaros. Many operators do not run trips on Wednesdays.

If you could choose just one place to swim in Bacalar, it would be Los Rápidos, south of town. Here, the lagoon narrows into a channel where a gentle current carries you, wearing a life jacket, alongside the stromatolites. These rocks are alive and must never be stepped on. Sunscreen, insect repellent, food, and coolers are prohibited. There is an admission fee and a waterfront restaurant. It is best to come in the afternoon.

Cenote Cocalitos, on the lagoon a 5- or 10-minute drive south of Bacalar, bills itself as a stromatolite sanctuary. Ropes and signs protect these formations. This type of living rock has existed on Earth for more than 3.5 billion years. The site has reopened after a two-year closure, with showers and a small refreshment stand. Admission costs 100 pesos per adult, and you can bring a picnic.

visits.text: If you arrive in Bernal in the late afternoon, save the Peña for the next day and explore the village. Since 2005, Bernal has held the Pueblo Mágico designation, a tourism distinction awarded by the Mexican government. The 18th-century Templo de San Sebastián Mártir has a Baroque facade of dressed stone. Nearby, El Castillo, a colonial-era building, houses the Museo de la Máscara and its more than 300 masks. Museum admission costs 30 pesos. The main square is the place to buy handicrafts.

activities.text: You’ll descend 25 m underground into the cellar at Freixenet de México, on the road to Cadereyta near Ezequiel Montes, about a 25-minute drive from Bernal. This Spanish sparkling wine producer established a presence in Mexico in 1979. One tour option includes a ride on the Uvabus, a small bus that travels through the 50 hectares of vineyards, with the Peña de Bernal as a backdrop. If you’re driving, leave the tasting to your passengers.

Easy at the start, vertical at the end: the climb up the Peña de Bernal changes character along the way. This 350 m-high rock is lava that cooled underground about 8.7 million years ago, then became exposed as the surrounding rock eroded. For the Otomí-Chichimeca people of Tolimán, an Indigenous people of the region, it is a sacred place. Their traditions have been inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2009. The trail leads to the viewpoints. The final 45 meters are a vertical rock face fitted with metal rungs: if you have no climbing experience, stop before this section.

Gorditas de maíz quebrado are the specialty to try in Bernal: thick griddle cakes made from cracked corn. The village’s artisanal liqueurs are also sold around the square. For dessert, the Museo del Dulce Mexicano showcases traditional Mexican candies. The 25-peso admission includes a tasting. Save this food stop for after your descent from the Peña, when you’ve worked up an appetite.

days_plan.itin_title: Querétaro in 5 Days: Bernal and the Sierra Gorda Missions

activities.text: In Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, Chapultepec means “on Grasshopper Hill.” No one knows whether the hill resembled a grasshopper or grasshoppers were abundant there. Walk through its first and oldest section, from the anthropology museum to the foot of the castle. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, 5 a.m. to 6 p.m., and closes on Mondays for maintenance.

days_plan.itin_title: Mexico City in 3 Days: Zócalo, Frida Kahlo, and Xochimilco

visits.text: Cabo Pulmo is a village of 300 inhabitants on the peninsula's east coast. Its coral reef, over 20,000 years old, is the only living hard coral reef in the entire Gulf of California - a unique ecosystem listed by UNESCO. In the 1990s, the village's fishing families themselves campaigned for a total ban on commercial fishing. Result: in 10 years, biomass increased 460%, a world record cited by the National Geographic Society. More than 800 marine species now inhabit the park's 7,000 hectares.

Snorkeling from Los Arbolitos beach requires no boat: wade into the water, swim 50 meters, and you're on the reef. Schools of jacks dense as clouds, groupers, resting turtles, foraging parrotfish. Waters are clear down to 30 meters depth.

activities.text: Boat excursions leave the village several times daily for the park's best dive spots: El Bajo, Los Morros, El Cantil. Certified local guides, modest rates, small groups. Book at the Cabo Pulmo Divers office on the main beach.

visits.text: Nearly 26 m long: that is the size of the Mural de la Batalla, Cacaxtla’s great mural. It depicts warriors dressed in jaguar skins, the victors, facing defeated warriors wearing bird headdresses and jade jewelry. It was painted around 650–700 by the Olmec-Xicalanca, a people whose city flourished between 650 and 900. An enormous roof protects it from sun and rain. The site is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last admission at 4 p.m.; foreign visitors pay 210 pesos, and flash photography is prohibited.

Next, head to Xochitécatl, 5 km away, an older religious center active mainly between 600 and 100 BC. Its largest structure is the Pirámide de las Flores, where archaeologists found around thirty burials, mostly of children, accompanied by offerings. The site is also known for its female figurines, linked to fertility and rain rituals. Bring a hat and water: you will be walking in full sun.

places.name: Cadereyta de Montes Que

visits.text: Quinta Fernando Schmoll in Cadereyta de Montes houses about 4,500 varieties of cacti and other succulents in its greenhouses. Landscape painter Fernando Schmoll and his wife, biologist Carolina Wagner, established it more than a century ago. Admission costs 50 pesos and includes a guided tour and a small cactus to take home. The greenhouses are open Tuesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wear long sleeves and pants to protect yourself from the spines.

An understated facade and an altarpiece laden with sculptures: the Parroquia de San Pedro y San Pablo in Cadereyta plays on contrast. This 18th-century church was built to evangelize the Otomi and Chichimeca, Indigenous peoples of the region. The altarpiece, a large sculpted decoration behind the altar, is in the Churrigueresque style, a highly ornate form of Spanish Baroque. Its clock dates from the era of Porfirio Díaz, president of Mexico in the late 19th century. The Quinta Schmoll greenhouses are an eight-minute walk from the main square.

visits.text: Campeche's historic center is one of Mexico's best-preserved and a UNESCO World Heritage site. Its 17th-century bastioned ramparts—built to repel Dutch and English pirates—still perfectly encircle the old colonial quarter. Each facade is painted a different color: the result is striking from the rampart walkway.

The Puerta de Mar—the sea gate—is the main entrance to the fortified city, where everything entering the city once landed. The Baluarte de la Soledad across the way houses a small museum of Mayan stelae from regional excavations.

activities.text: The malecón runs along the sea west of the ramparts. At sunset, locals gather here: bikes, families, jícama vendors. It's one of Mexico's best malecóns—calm, clean, with no hotel towers blocking the view.

Dinner in one of the converted colonial houses in the historic center—Campeche is famous for its pan de cazón, a tortilla stack layered with shark meat. Campechan cuisine blends Mayan and Caribbean influences with surprising finesse.

visits.text: Cancún's hotel zone is a 22.5-kilometer strip shaped like the number 7, squeezed between the Caribbean Sea and Nichupté Lagoon. The north side of the island—Bahía de Mujeres—has the calmest water, perfect for a gentle first swim after your flight.

Nichupté Lagoon runs along the entire back of the hotel zone. Tour operators offer sunset boat trips through mangroves, with pelicans and iguanas bathed in golden late-afternoon light. A lovely introduction to Mexico, far from the beach crowds.

activities.text: Get settled, then grab tacos in the downtown area (El Centro)—away from the hotel zone, prices and quality change dramatically. A plate of cochinita pibil for 80 pesos is the real Yucatán welcome.
First sunset on the beach on the north side—low-angle light, turquoise water, no strong currents. Bring biodegradable sunscreen: its use is regulated along the entire coast.

activities.text: You will land at Cancún International Airport, where this rental car itinerary begins. Before leaving Mexico, you will need to show your receipt for the Quintana Roo tourist tax, which is mandatory for foreign visitors. Pay it online through the Mexican authorities’ official portal as soon as you arrive. Then drive to Chiquilá, about 2 hours away. Set off promptly: France Diplomatie advises against driving at night.

places.name: Capulálpam de Méndez Oax

visits.text: The ceiling alone makes a stop at Templo de San Mateo, the church in Capulálpam de Méndez, worthwhile. It is an alfarje: a decorative arrangement of wooden beams and planks, a technique brought from Spain. The church dates from the 16th century. It preserves several altarpieces from the 17th and 18th centuries, large carved decorations placed behind the altar. Capulálpam holds the Pueblo Mágico designation, awarded by the Mexican government to villages of interest to tourists: stroll through the village after your visit.

activities.text: If you have never tried a temazcal, a traditional Mexican steam bath, the Centro de Medicina Tradicional in Capulálpam offers them. Massages and herbal remedies are also available. The center is affiliated with an organization of traditional Zapotec practitioners, founded here in 1995, that brings together about 45 healers. It shares its premises with the village clinic. Its affordable treatments are available to visitors. Book when you arrive and mention any health conditions before your session.

In 1775, after the discovery of the Dolores mine, Capulálpam de Méndez opened its first hacienda de beneficio, an estate where gold and silver were separated from ore. Today, the village is best known for its mountain forests, recognized in 2002 by WWF, an international nature conservation organization. To see them from above, climb to the Cruz Blanca lookout. The ecotourism center also arranges a cave visit and a crossing of a cable bridge over the Los Molinos River.

visits.text: Chapultepec Castle tells the story of more than a century of Mexican history. Construction began in 1785 for a Spanish viceroy, and it later became a military academy. On September 13, 1847, young cadets known as the Niños Héroes (“Child Heroes”) died here defending it against the United States Army. Maximilian, Emperor of Mexico, and his wife Charlotte lived here from 1864 to 1867. He had the avenue connecting the castle to the city center laid out; it is now Paseo de la Reforma. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; on Sundays, admission stops after 10,000 visitors.

places.name: Catedral Metropolitana Ciudad de México Cmx

visits.text: The highlight of the Catedral Metropolitana, which borders the north side of the Zócalo, is the Altar de los Reyes. This altarpiece, a large sculpted backdrop behind the altar, is made of gilded cedar and rises 25 m. It is nicknamed “la cueva dorada,” the golden cave. Construction lasted from 1573 to 1813, which explains the mix of styles, from Gothic to Neoclassical. Like the rest of Mexico City, the cathedral is sinking, and its towers were leaning. From 1993 to 1998, engineers excavated beneath it so it would settle evenly. Be discreet during Mass.

visits.text: The Zona del Silencio: compasses that wander, phones that lose their signal, meteorites said to fall here more than elsewhere. The story goes that a PEMEX engineer named the place in the 1960s after finding no radio signal on his equipment. Science has still not settled on an explanation.

activities.text: Stargazing from the Mapimí Biosphere Reserve, far from any light pollution, is the strongest experience of this itinerary. The Complejo Ecoturístico La Zona del Silencio offers camping nights with telescope observation. Book a guide: the desert trails are unmarked.

activities.text: Pink patches at the water’s surface: these are the flamingos of the Celestún ría. A ría is an estuary where freshwater mixes with saltwater from the Gulf of Mexico. Flamingos are most numerous here from November through March. They are born white: their color comes from pigments in their food, such as shrimp larvae. The boat tour lasts 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes, taking you between Bird Island and the mangrove forest, which grows in saltwater. Expect to pay around 1,800 pesos per six-passenger boat.

You will end the day on Celestún’s beach, on the Gulf of Mexico. The village relies mainly on fishing and salt production, and tourism is gaining ground. The coast faces west, so the sun sets over the sea. Stay for sunset, then have dinner in the village, since you are spending the night here.

visits.text: The El Fuerte → Bahuichivo/Cerocahui journey by Chepe train takes about 6 hours. Sit on the right side (if departing from Los Mochis/El Fuerte): the best canyon views are on this side. The train starts at sea level, crosses tropical plains, climbs into oak forest, then into the pines of the Sierra Tarahumara. The landscape changes completely every hour. The train's full route includes 86 tunnels and 37 viaducts.

Cerocahui is a village in the sierra built around a 17th-century Jesuit mission. From the viewpoint above the village, you look down into Urique Canyon—1,800 meters deep, one of the deepest in the Barrancas del Cobre. Allow for a round trip by vehicle from Cerocahui to reach the viewpoint. Below, invisible from here, are the village of Urique and the river.

activities.text: The descent on foot or by 4x4 to the bottom of Urique canyon is an experience in itself. The village at the bottom is tropical, with mangoes and lemon trees, while the canyon rim is temperate forest. Local operators organize the descent from Cerocahui.

visits.text: Listen closely: howler monkeys live in the forest surrounding Chacchoben. The site’s Maya name means “the place of red corn.” A loop trail passes three restored pyramids; some retain traces of red paint, protected from the sun by roofs. Archaeologist Peter Harrison reported the site in 1972 after spotting its hills from a helicopter. Arrive early: tours come from the Costa Maya cruise port.

places.name: Chetumal Roo

visits.text: After so many ruins, Chetumal’s Museo de la Cultura Maya helps connect what you have seen. It is described as the state’s most comprehensive museum on Maya civilization, covering its origins, development, and daily life. It displays original artifacts and reproductions. If you arrive late from Kohunlich, save it for the next morning, before your flight. The city itself was almost entirely destroyed by Hurricane Janet in 1955.

As you enter Chetumal, you will pass a modern Maya pyramid bearing statues of the Spaniard Gonzalo Guerrero, his wife Zazil Há, and their children. This is the Monumento Cuna del Mestizaje, the “cradle of mixed heritage.” Its name celebrates the union of two peoples in one family. Stop for a few minutes: the monument stands along the road into the city.

places.name: Chihuahua

visits.text: The Chepe train from Divisadero to Chihuahua takes about 5 hours. Upon arrival, Quinta Luz—Pancho Villa's former residence—is the must-see museum. The 48-room house remains as it was at Villa's death in 1923. In the courtyard: the black Dodge riddled with bullets in which he was assassinated in Parral—the bullet holes are original. Inside: his saddles, pistols, photos, bedroom. His legally recognized widow, Luz Corral, lived here until her death in 1981.

A monumental fresco from the 1960s by Aarón Piña Mora covers the walls of the inner courtyard of the Palacio de Gobierno de Chihuahua, telling the history of the state of Chihuahua from its origins. The baroque cathedral on the Plaza de Armas, built between 1725 and 1826, is one of the most beautiful in northern Mexico.

activities.text: Return flight to Mexico City or your destination from Chihuahua International Airport (CUU). Domestic flights to CDMX take 1 hour 30 minutes. The airport is 20 minutes from the city center by taxi.

activities.text: Chiquilá, a small mainland port across from Holbox, marks the end of the road: visitors’ cars are not allowed on the island. Leave yours in a parking lot near the dock. Two high-speed ferry companies, Holbox Express and 9 Hermanos, alternate departures from early morning until evening. The 13 km crossing takes 20 to 25 minutes. Travel light: Holbox has sandy streets.

You’ll take a morning boat back to Chiquilá to pick up your car in the port parking lot. The drive to Río Lagartos then takes about 2 hours 30 minutes. A stop in Tizimín breaks up the journey halfway. Fill up on gas and bring water before setting off. Aim to arrive at the Las Coloradas saltworks in the early afternoon, when the sun makes their pink color more intense.

places.name: Cholula Pue

visits.text: A wooded hill crowned with a church? It is actually the Gran Pirámide de Cholula, whose Nahuatl name, Tlachihualtepetl, means “built mountain.” Its base measures about 300 m by 315 m. According to Guinness World Records, it is the world’s largest pyramid by volume, at more than 4.45 million m³, compared with about 2.5 million for the Great Pyramid of Giza. Start at the Patio de los Altares, the former main entrance.

Cholula’s finest moment awaits at the top of the pyramid, in front of the Santuario de Nuestra Señora de los Remedios. The Spanish built this church in 1594, above the ancient temple. Lightning has struck it several times, and in the early colonial period, people saw this as the wrath of the ancient rain goddess. Climb up in the late afternoon: in clear weather, Popocatépetl stands out to the west.

The Convento de San Gabriel was built on the site of a temple dedicated to Quetzalcóatl, the feathered serpent god. Indigenous workers built it entirely under the direction of the friar Toribio de Alcaraz. On the main square, the parish church of San Pedro has a dome in the Churrigueresque style, a highly ornate Spanish Baroque style, pierced by eight windows. End the day in this square before having dinner in town.

activities.text: Explore the Cholula pyramid from the outside: according to INAH, its tunnels remain closed to the public until further notice. Beginning in 1931, archaeologists dug about 8 km of passageways to explore the structure’s interior. Do not plan to go down into these passages: the reopening announced in March 2026 has not been confirmed by the National Institute of Anthropology and History.

places.name: Mexico City

visits.text: In Mexico City, explore Roma Norte on foot: Colima and Orizaba streets are lined with old houses, cafés, and galleries. At Plaza Río de Janeiro, look at the façades surrounding the garden and the central fountain. Continue along the neighboring streets to observe the balconies and entrances of the district's buildings.

In Mexico City's Condesa district, walk along Avenida Ámsterdam, whose oval route surrounds Parque México. Look at the Art Deco façades, then enter the park to see its tree-lined paths and open-air theater. The cafés on nearby streets provide a place to take a break after your walk.

Mexico City's Zócalo is one of the world's largest squares—57,000 square meters, on the site of Tenochtitlan, the ancient Aztec capital. The National Palace on the east side occupies the site of Moctezuma's palace. Inside, Diego Rivera's murals (1929–1935) trace 3,000 years of Mexican history across 1,200 square meters of walls. Free admission.

The Templo Mayor (excavated since 1978) is Tenochtitlan's main pyramid, uncovered directly beneath the historic center. The adjoining museum displays statuettes and objects from the eagle's tomb. Allow at least an hour.

activities.text: Drive to Mexico City (about 2 hours from Cholula, depending on traffic). Settle into the Roma or Condesa neighborhoods—two Art Deco districts with excellent cafés and restaurants, ideal as a base for your last day.

First evening in Mexico City in Condesa: tacos de canasta, mezcal, and terraces under the jacarandas (February–April) or sweetgum trees. A city at a dizzying scale—22 million people—but the central neighborhoods are on a human scale.

Coyoacán in the afternoon—Mexico City's most charming neighborhood. Frida Kahlo's House (Casa Azul) is painted cobalt and turquoise blue and showcases her works, studio, and life. Online reservation required. The Coyoacán craft market across the street sells reproductions of pre-Hispanic ceramics.

Xochimilco as an alternative: plan a round trip during the day from central Mexico City. The trajineras (flower-decorated boats propelled with poles) travel through a network of preserved Aztec canals, one of the few remnants of the ancient lake city. On weekends, Mexican families fill the canals with their own boats and music. A floating celebration.

activities.text: Pick up your rental car in Mexico City early in the morning: France Diplomatie recommends driving during daylight hours and using toll highways. It also advises against visiting several suburban municipalities, including Ecatepec and Nezahualcóyotl. To avoid Ecatepec, leave Mexico City on the 16.5 km Peñón-Texcoco toll highway, then continue to Teotihuacán via Tepexpan. Fill up at a gas station in the city and keep pesos in cash for tolls.

Return to Mexico City via toll highway 150D, which connects Puebla to the capital. France Diplomatie advises against travel only on its other section, from Puebla east toward Orizaba, which is not on your route. Leave early and travel during daylight, fill up in town, then return the car in Mexico City.

places.name: Ciudad Valles

visits.text: The descent from Real de Catorce to the Huasteca Potosina is one of Mexico's most spectacular landscape transitions. You go from 2,750 m above sea level in a cactus desert to 100 m in dense tropical jungle. The vegetation changes every half hour. Keep your eyes open along the road: it winds through gorges, crosses rivers and passes through villages where women still wear the embroidered huipil of the Teenek.

Las Pozas in Xilitla is the wild project of Edward James—an eccentric British poet, patron of the surrealists and friend of Dalí and Magritte. Allow for a round trip in a day from Ciudad Valles. In 1962, after a frost killed his 29,000 orchids, he began building concrete structures in the jungle. Staircases leading to the sky. Doors opening onto nothing. Flower-shaped columns 10 meters high. He continued until his death in 1984 without ever finishing. The garden covers 37 hectares—9 of sculptures, the rest primary forest. It was declared a national artistic monument in 2012. Book your time slot ahead: daily visitor numbers are limited.

Puente de Dios—the Bridge of God—is a natural limestone arch beneath which a river flows through a turquoise pool. Water filters through the rock, taking on an unreal blue-green color. You swim beneath the arch. The parking lot is approximately 57 km from Ciudad Valles, a 1-hour drive. Access is on foot from this parking lot—allow 20 minutes along the trail.

The Cascadas de Micos are a series of nine waterfalls spread over about 500 meters amid tropical vegetation. It's approximately 34 km from Ciudad Valles, a 40-minute drive. Each pool is suitable for swimming—some allow jumps from rocks 3 to 8 meters high. The water is warm (27–28°C in summer). Allow 2 hours to explore the entire site.

activities.text: Arrival in Ciudad Valles in late afternoon—it's the logistical base for the Huasteca. The town itself is uninteresting, but it's where the activity providers, Huastecan restaurants, and hotels are concentrated. Get settled and organize tomorrow's excursions: Xilitla and Tamul can be combined in a single day from Ciudad Valles with a 7 a.m. departure.

In the afternoon, take a boat from the Tanchachin landing to reach Tamul waterfall by traveling upstream on the Santa María River. Allow for a round trip by road from Ciudad Valles to the landing. Tamul is the highest waterfall in the state of San Luis Potosí—a 105-meter drop surrounded by limestone cliffs covered in vegetation. The boat trip takes about 45 minutes in each direction.

If you have an extra half-day, the Sótano de las Golondrinas is one of Mexico's most mesmerizing natural phenomena. It's a vertical sinkhole 376 meters deep, 135 meters wide at the opening. Every morning at sunrise, tens of thousands of white swifts with black backs spiral upward—a living vortex rising for several minutes. Access from Ciudad Valles takes 2 hours—it's an excursion to schedule very early in the morning.

activities.text: Head up Avenida Álvaro Obregón, a major thoroughfare in Colonia Roma (the Roma neighborhood), with metal benches beneath tall trees. The neighborhood was developed starting in the 1900s for wealthy families, during the presidency of Porfirio Díaz. On Plaza Río de Janeiro, a replica of Michelangelo’s David stands near a fountain. Nearby, the Casa de las Brujas (“House of Witches”) dates from 1908. Alfonso Cuarón’s film Roma is set in this neighborhood in the 1970s. In the evening, take a rideshare back, as recommended by France Diplomatie.

activities.text: In 1910, President Porfirio Díaz inaugurated a horse racing track where Condesa stands today. The track fell out of use during the Mexican Revolution, but Avenida Amsterdam still follows its curve, which explains its loop. Parque México occupies the former center of the track. Many of the surrounding Art Deco buildings, such as Edificio Basurto, date from the 1920s through the 1940s. Condesa means “countess”: the name recalls the Countess of Miravalle, who owned this land. Walk the Amsterdam loop, then cross the park.

visits.text: The center of Coyoacán has retained the feel of an old town, with its two squares and 16th-century church. In Nahuatl, its name means “the place of those who have coyotes.” Two bronze coyotes by sculptor Gabriel Ponzanelli adorn the fountain in Jardín Centenario. This garden was once the courtyard of San Juan Bautista Church, built between 1520 and 1552. After the conquest, Hernán Cortés made Coyoacán the first capital of New Spain, the Spanish colony, from 1521 to 1523. The garden is a 10-minute walk from the Casa Azul.

activities.text: Finish at Mercado de Coyoacán, the neighborhood market, built in 1956 by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, the architect of the anthropology museum. In the evening, street vendors sell tostadas, crisp corn tortillas with toppings, around the central squares. According to the Coyoacán local government, the center receives about 70,000 visitors each weekend: come on a weekday if you prefer a quieter atmosphere. In the evening, stay on busy streets and take a rideshare back.

visits.text: The sand is so white you mistake it for snow at first glance. The Dunas de Yeso of Cuatro Ciénegas formed from salts deposited by the ancient Tethys Sea. Only a few rare areas of this type exist in the world. The highest dune, nicknamed 'El Castillo,' rises to 12 meters and offers a view of the surrounding mountains. Protected zone: stay on marked trails.

Blue to a point that looks unreal, the Poza Azul is fed by underground aquifers in the Cuatro Ciénegas valley. It belongs to a group of about 200 protected pools, all of exceptional purity. Swimming is forbidden: you look at the pool from the wooden platforms built along the edge and from the raised viewpoint.

The stromatolites of Cuatro Ciénegas are living organisms that invented photosynthesis billions of years ago. NASA studies primitive life forms here to understand how life could have developed on other planets. The Biosphere Reserve, protected since 1994, is home to more than 150 endemic animal and plant species.

If the reserve leaves you wanting more, the centro histórico of Cuatro Ciénegas recalls that the town is the birthplace of Venustiano Carranza, president of Mexico from 1915 to 1920. The Museo Venustiano Carranza in his birthplace tells this history. The Plaza de Armas in the evening is lively and well-lit.

activities.text: Walk to 'El Castillo,' the big 12-meter dune: from the top, the sierra mountains frame the white expanse 360°. No fixed trail—explore freely. Arrive early morning or late afternoon to avoid the midday glare.

To swim you have to leave the Poza Azul and go to the Río Los Mezquites, inside the same protected area, where the water stays cool even in high summer. The Poza de la Becerra, warmer, also allows swimming and camping at the water's edge. No sunscreen and no soap in the water, the signs on site repeat it everywhere.

Sunset over the Cuatro Ciénegas Biosphere Reserve turns the desert into a palette of reds and oranges against white sand. Rent a bike at the entrance to the village and ride out to the Río Los Mezquites, the river that crosses the basin and gives the best camera angles in the area.

places.name: Divisadero

visits.text: Divisadero is THE viewpoint of the Barrancas del Cobre. From the train station, you look down into three canyons simultaneously: Urique, Tararecua, and Cobre, with a 1,800-meter vertical drop. The Barrancas del Cobre form a system of six canyons whose total area is four times larger than the American Grand Canyon. The Chepe stops here for a few minutes—step out onto the platform even if you're not staying.

At the canyon's edge, Tarahumara women sell their handicrafts: woven grass baskets, fabric dolls, pine bowls. The Rarámuri—their name in their own language, meaning “foot runners”—live in the mountains and caves of the sierra. They're the ultra-marathon runners in leather sandals whom the world knows from the book Born to Run. Buy directly from them.

activities.text: The Parque Aventura Barrancas del Cobre offers the ZipRider—2.5 km of zipline over the canyon, descending at 80 km/h, starting at 2,400 meters elevation. It's one of the longest ziplines in the world. The park also offers a circuit of seven linked ziplines with rope bridges, and a via ferrata. Book upon arrival—slots fill quickly in high season.

visits.text: Durango is a colonial city less well known than its neighbors, and that's precisely its appeal. Its historic center is intact, its Plaza de Armas large and open, its 17th-century baroque cathedral restrained and elegant. The city sits at 1,880 meters elevation in a basin surrounded by the Sierra Madre—the air is dry, nights cool. Wander through the city center without a set plan: the street markets and colonial arcades are worth lingering over.

The film studios in the desert around Durango have served as sets for dozens of westerns—Mexican and American—since the 1950s. Productions involving Sergio Leone, John Wayne, and Anthony Quinn were filmed here. Several sets still stand a few kilometers from town: saloons, sheriff's offices, dusty streets. Some offer daytime tours.

activities.text: If you stumble upon an escaramuza charra, don't pass it by. This Mexican women's rodeo—women galloping in traditional dresses, performing synchronized figures on horseback without saddles—is one of Mexico's most impressive spectacles. Charrerías (rodeos) take place on weekends in the lienzos charros of northern cities. Ask at the tourist office when you arrive.

places.name: Dzibilchaltún Yuc

visits.text: The Templo de las Siete Muñecas, or Temple of the Seven Dolls, was hidden beneath a newer temple. It takes its name from seven small figurines found when it was discovered in the 1950s. At Dzibilchaltún, 16 km north of Mérida, crowds come to watch the sun rise through its doorways at the spring and fall equinoxes. Yet there is no evidence that the Maya intended this alignment. The site is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last entry at 4 p.m.

A cenote where swimming is off-limits: at the center of the Dzibilchaltún ruins, the Xlacah cenote is protected. Divers have recovered carved bones, wooden objects, and, above all, vessels, evidence that this was a place of worship. The site also preserves the ruins of a 16th-century Spanish church. Finish at the Ichkaantijoo museum, open in 2026: it displays more than 300 Maya artifacts from the region, and admission is included in your ticket.

visits.text: Ek’ Balam impresses more with its sculptures than its size. The Acropolis, the site’s large pyramid, stands about 32 m tall. On its fourth level, the tomb of King Ukit Kan Le’k Tok’, who ruled from 770, opens through a doorway shaped like a monster’s mouth, perhaps a jaguar’s. This doorway is modeled in stucco, a lime-based plaster. Winged stucco figures surround it. Budget for two tickets: one from INAH, the national institute responsible for the sites, and a Yucatán tax that is higher for foreigners.

Two stone walls surround Ek’ Balam, yet some sections seem too low to stop an army. Archaeologists are unsure: were they real defenses or simply boundaries restricting access to the center? Enter from the south, following the sacbé, Mayan for “white road”: an ancient raised road. An arch marks the entrance through the wall. The Oval Palace, set on a rectangular base, and the ball court round out the visit. The site is open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last admission at 4 p.m.

activities.text: You’ll reach X’Canché Cenote along a 1.5 km trail from the ruins, on foot or by rental bike. A cenote is a natural sinkhole formed in limestone and filled with fresh water. This one forms a circle of water about 40 meters across, roughly 15 meters below ground level. Local residents have managed it since 2002 as a community project, offering swimming, rappelling down a rope, zip-lining over the water, hammocks, and a restaurant. Save your swim for after the ruins.

visits.text: El Fuerte is an understated colonial Pueblo Mágico in Sinaloa state—the town hall, the 17th-century church, colorful façades around the plaza. The town is also known for a persistent local legend: it's said to be the birthplace of Diego de la Vega, alias Zorro. The regional museum takes this seriously.

The El Fuerte River flows below the town—boat trips are available. Migratory birds, kingfishers and herons: the wildlife is remarkable. It is also an opportunity to see the way of life of the Mayo communities living along the banks.

activities.text: In the evening, prepare for your climb into the canyons. El Fuerte station is the departure point for the Chepe. Ask at your hotel about tomorrow's schedule—the train leaves early in the morning. Local gastronomy is also worth exploring: machaca with eggs (dried shredded meat sautéed with eggs), Tarahumara tamales, and coricos (wheat flour cookies) are regional specialties.

visits.text: Ensenada's malecón stretches for several kilometers along the bay. This is where the fish taco stands cluster - a local specialty: fried fish or shrimp in tempura batter, crema, salsa verde, crisp cabbage in a corn tortilla. Show up at the port's fish market early in the morning to watch fishermen unload their catch.

La Bufadora is a natural marine blowhole in the cliffs of the Punta Banda peninsula; plan for a round trip from Ensenada. Water rushes into an underwater cavity and shoots up to 27 meters high at high tide. It is one of the most powerful marine blowholes in the Northern Hemisphere. The access road follows the bay—it is worth the trip in its own right.
Head up to the El Mirador viewpoint north of town; plan for a round trip from Ensenada. A 180° view of the bay and port—the best view of Ensenada. Ideal in the late afternoon when the light is low.

activities.text: Ensenada has built a reputation as Baja California's craft beer capital. Several craft breweries have opened downtown—the scene is young and experimental, and prices remain affordable. Spend the evening lingering here before hitting the road tomorrow.

places.name: Felipe Carrillo Puerto Roo

visits.text: “The talking cross”: that is the meaning of the name Santuario de la Cruz Parlante, in Felipe Carrillo Puerto. During the Caste War, the city was called Chan Santa Cruz. Maya rebels believed that this cross conveyed God’s voice to guide their struggle. Its followers called themselves the Cruzo’ob, “those of the cross.” In this region, crosses are often dressed in huipiles, embroidered blouses. Enter quietly: this is still a sanctuary.

visits.text: Discovered in 1843, the Grutas de García feature 16 chambers of stalactites and stalagmites in a 2-km network carved into rock about 60 million years ago. In the 'El Árbol de Navidad' gallery, the formations take shapes that would put any decorated Christmas tree to shame. Bring a light jacket: the cave stays cool year-round.

activities.text: Take the 650-meter cable car: five minutes suspended 200 meters up to reach the cave entrance, with a plunging view over the Nuevo León desert. The walk up also exists (about 1 hour), but the cable car is worth the price. Open Tue-Sun, ticket office closes at 3pm.

places.name: Guadalajara

visits.text: Hospicio Cabañas is the main reason to come to Guadalajara. Built in 1810 as an orphanage and hospital, this UNESCO-listed complex houses in its chapel 57 murals by José Clemente Orozco, painted 1938–1939. The showstopper: 'El Hombre de Fuego' (Man of Fire) beneath the dome—a figure consumed by flames, considered by Orozco himself his masterwork. Take time to lie on the benches and gaze at the ceiling.

Guadalajara's Metropolitan Cathedral is recognizable from afar by its two blue azulejo towers. Construction began 1541, in hybrid baroque-neoclassical style. The interior holds canvases attributed to Murillo and Rubens. Plaza de la Liberación in front links four successive plazas all the way to the Hospicio.

Tlaquepaque, technically an independent town absorbed by the metropolis, is Guadalajara's artisan quarter. Pedestrian Calle Independencia is lined with 19th-century mansions converted to galleries. Blown glass, talavera, and Huichol beadwork pieces (colored glass beads on wooden figures—work taking several weeks) are the signature purchases. El Parián, the round plaza ringed by restaurants, pulses with mariachi groups morning to night.

The Mercado San Juan de Dios is a huge covered market—3,000 stalls on three levels. Electronics, clothing, crafts, jewelry, and on every corner fondas serving torta ahogada, the sandwich drowned in spicy red sauce, Guadalajara's signature dish. Birria, the goat stew, is eaten here too, as quesabirrias topped with melted cheese.

The town of Tequila sits 65 km from Guadalajara, at the foot of the volcano of the same name. It's a pueblo mágico surrounded by UNESCO-listed blue agave fields. Agaves used for tequila production take 7–12 years to mature—you see them stretching endlessly, their blue-green lance-shaped leaves under Jalisco sun.

activities.text: Evening in Chapultepec neighborhood, Colonia Americana. Avenida Chapultepec is Guadalajara's hippest corridor—independent cafés, cocktail bars, galleries spilling onto sidewalks. The vibe picks up from 7 PM when students and young professionals fill the terraces.

Half-day excursion to Tequila. Visit a distillery—La Rojeña by José Cuervo is the oldest in Mexico, but the smaller craft distilleries are often more instructive. Tasting a blanco, a reposado, and an añejo shows how the spirit changes as it ages in oak barrels.

Stroll through downtown Tequila after the distillery. The main plaza, giant multicolored 'TEQUILA' letters for photos, jimador (agave harvester) sculptures, and a cantarito—the local cocktail served in earthenware pottery with tequila and grapefruit juice. At 9 PM, the priest emerges from the temple and rings the three bells while all the townspeople rise wherever they are.

visits.text: Guanajuato wedges itself into a ravine. Cars navigate underground tunnels carved from former dried riverbeds—it's a city with entirely subterranean downtown traffic. Houses stack up the slopes, each facade painted a different color. Take time to get lost upon arrival.

Jardín de la Unión is the triangular plaza at the heart of everything. Terraces, musicians, and facing you Teatro Juárez—inaugurated in 1903 with Doric columns and statues of Greek muses perched on the pediment. The Belle Époque interior is equally sumptuous. Visit if it's open.

Callejón del Beso is the city's narrowest alley—68 centimeters between the two facing balconies. The legend: Ana, a noble's daughter, and Carlos, a miner, met balcony-to-balcony at night. Her father caught them and stabbed his daughter in her lover's arms. Since then, kissing on the third step guarantees seven years of happiness.

The University of Guanajuato was founded in the 17th century. Its white and ochre neoclassical, neo-baroque façade descends into the town in monumental staircases. It is the symbol of the city—it appears in every travel photo.

Alhóndiga de Granaditas was an 18th-century granary. In 1810, Spanish troops barricaded themselves inside against Miguel Hidalgo's 20,000-strong insurgent army. A miner nicknamed El Pípila strapped a stone slab to his back for bullet protection and set the doors ablaze. The city fell. It's the Independence War's first turning point. Today it's a regional museum, closed Mondays.

Climb to Monumento al Pípila for the panoramic view. The pink statue depicts the miner holding his torch above the city. From here you see colored rooftops stacking up the hills, church domes, tunnels disappearing underground. This is THE Guanajuato photo. Climb via stairs or take the funicular from downtown.

Mercado Hidalgo is a large industrial-style metal hall built in 1910—originally intended as a train station. Inside, two levels of fruit, spice, souvenir, and small restaurant stalls. Downstairs vegetables and local specialties, upstairs artisans. Enchiladas mineras, Guanajuato's signature chicken-and-red-sauce dish, are eaten here.

Diego Rivera House-Museum marks the painter's 1886 birthplace. The first floors recreate the period bourgeois apartment with original furniture. The rest hosts temporary exhibitions and a selection of his works. Small but well-curated.

activities.text: Drive through the tunnels upon arrival—one of Mexico's most unusual experiences. Several kilometers of lit two-lane underground galleries, with subterranean roundabouts and exits opening into neighborhood hearts.

Evening, catch a callejoneada starting from Jardín de la Unión. Students in period costume—the estudiantinas—guide groups through the alleys singing ballads and recounting city legends. Men receive clay jugs with drinks, women receive roses. It ends with dancing in the cobblestone streets.

Explore the tunnels on foot—several pedestrian passages cross the city underground, accessing neighborhoods otherwise unreachable in a straight line. It's a labyrinth requiring some orientation but revealing interior courtyards and secret passages at the end.

Wander the stepped callejones above downtown. Alleys climb to residential neighborhoods where houses are painted bright blue, orange, yellow. The higher you climb, the fewer tourists. Improvised miradors between houses offer plunging city views.

places.name: Guelatao de Juárez Oax

visits.text: Benito Juárez, president of Mexico from 1858 to 1872, was born in Guelatao de Juárez on March 21, 1806. Near the town hall, a small museum brings together images, statues, and objects relating to his life, and a replica of his home is open to visitors. A bronze statue depicts him seated. Beside it, his words appear in bronze letters: “El respeto al derecho ajeno es la paz,” “Respect for the rights of others is peace.”

Continue to Ixtlán de Juárez, a few minutes’ drive away, at an elevation above 2,000 m. Its Templo de Santo Tomás Apóstol dates from the 16th century. The village’s ecotourism center offers zip-lining and trails through the cloud forest, a damp mountain forest often shrouded in mist. A glass-floored observation deck overlooks this forest. The community market sells honey, organic coffee, and forest products: a good stop for a snack.

activities.text: Pines and oaks surround Guelatao’s small lagoon, known as Laguna Encantada, the “enchanted lagoon.” At the water’s edge, a metal statue depicts a young shepherd and his sheep, evoking Juárez’s childhood. Walk around the lagoon before continuing toward Capulálpam.

places.name: Guerrero Negro

visits.text: The San Quintín → Guerrero Negro drive (about 5 hours) is the road trip's most spectacular leg. Highway 1 cuts straight through the central desert: 15-meter cardon cacti, swirls of ochre dust, absolute silence. Cross the 28th parallel, which marks the border between Baja California and Baja California Sur—there's a monumental eagle at the roadside.

Upon arrival, take a look at the Guerrero Negro saltworks. Operated by Exportadora de Sal (a Mexican-Japanese Mitsubishi joint venture), they produce about 9 million tonnes of salt annually. The evaporation ponds are so vast they're visible from space. The town takes its name from an American whaling ship—the Black Warrior—that ran aground here in 1858.

activities.text: If you arrive during whale season (December–April), inquire on arrival about booking a lancha trip on Laguna Ojo de Liebre the following morning. It is the largest of the three breeding lagoons for eastern Pacific gray whales—up to 2,000 individuals gather here each winter to give birth. Pangas generally depart at 8 a.m. or 11 a.m. for a 3-hour trip.

visits.text: The people of Hidalgo watch the climbers scrambling over the limestone walls of Potrero Chico while sipping a beer—and find it highly entertaining. This canyon in the Sierra del Fraile boasts limestone cliffs up to 600 meters high. Potrero Chico is an international climbing destination with routes graded 5.7 to 5.14.

activities.text: Even if you've never set foot on a wall, the guides at SouthernXposure (local reference for 18 years) offer beginner courses on short, well-equipped routes. The golden months for climbing are November-February; in summer the heat shuts down the walls. Non-climber option: hike the canyon to the natural pools that locals frequent in the evening.

visits.text: Not a meter of asphalt: Holbox has sandy streets, and people get around on foot, by bike, or by golf cart. The island stretches for about forty kilometers and is no more than two kilometers wide. Its name comes from the Maya language and means “black hole.” Since 1994, the island has been part of the Yum Balam protected area. Rent a bike in the village for your entire stay: it is the easiest way to reach Punta Cocos.

On a moonless night, stay at Punta Cocos after sunset. In this lagoon at the western tip of Holbox, you can see bioluminescence: light emitted by tiny living organisms in the water. The darker the night, the easier it is to see. Arrive in time for sunset first. Then turn off your lights and let your eyes adjust to the darkness for about 10 minutes.

activities.text: The main draw of Holbox’s northern beach is its tranquility, far from the coast’s large resorts. Three-quarters of the island consists of mangroves and deserted beaches: a short walk is all it takes to leave the village behind. Kitesurfing, which involves riding a board pulled by a large kite, is among the activities offered on the island. According to Holbox hoteliers, the tip of Cape Catoche acts as a natural barrier against sargassum, the floating seaweed from the Atlantic. Go for a swim in the late afternoon, then head to Punta Cocos.

Roughly from June through September, whale sharks gather off Holbox, drawn by warmer water. Sightings are most frequent in July and August. Agencies on the island arrange guided boat trips: you swim alongside these enormous fish with a mask and snorkel. The area is part of the Yum Balam protected area, which the authorities monitor during the season. Book the day before, and take this trip instead of the three-island tour.

Holbox agencies call this outing the three-island tour, “tres islas” in Spanish. The boat first heads to Isla Pasión, an islet with beaches 10 minutes from the port. It then continues to Isla de los Pájaros, the island of birds, covered in mangroves and cacti. Boardwalks and two observation platforms let you watch the birds, including flamingos, without approaching them. The final stop is the ojo de agua of Yalahau, a freshwater spring that local tradition describes as a fountain of youth.

activities.text: Leave the car behind and hop into a mototaxi, a motorized tricycle with a bench seat, to tour the cenotes of Homún. A cenote is a natural sinkhole filled with fresh water. Homún sits on the edge of the Chicxulub crater, formed by the impact of an enormous meteorite. The region’s cenotes follow this edge in an arc: this is the Anillo de Cenotes, the ring of cenotes. In Homún, around thirty are open to the public. Allow about 3 hours for three cenotes, and expect to pay 300 to 350 pesos for a mototaxi carrying up to four people.

Stalactites hang above the water in the Santa Rosa cenote, beneath a broad natural vault. In Homún, each cenote has its own shape: Yaxbacaltún is open to the sky, while Canunchén is a cave lit through a large opening. To protect the water, do not apply sunscreen or insect repellent before swimming. Many cenotes provide life jackets; Santa Rosa charges 280 pesos per adult.

visits.text: It is hard to believe that nature alone carved the Prismas Basálticos de Santa María Regla, near Huasca de Ocampo. These basalt columns, often with five or six sides, reach heights of 30 to 40 m. They formed as lava flows slowly cooled around 2.5 million years ago: as the rock cooled, it cracked into regular prisms. The German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt drew them in 1803. Admission costs 100 pesos and includes the footbridge, overlooks, and access to the waterfalls.

To see where silver was separated from the ore extracted from the mines, visit Hacienda Santa María Regla, next to the prisms. Pedro Romero de Terreros, the wealthy operator of the Real del Monte mines, had it built around 1760 beside the river because flat ground was needed, and none could be found on the slopes of Real del Monte. You can see courtyards made of volcanic stone, a small chapel, tunnels, and La Rosa waterfall. Tours run daily from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Many visitors believe it is dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel, but the Parroquia de San Juan Bautista de Huasca de Ocampo is dedicated to Saint John the Baptist. Augustinian monks from Atotonilco el Grande founded it in the 16th century. In 2001, Huasca became Mexico’s first “Pueblo Mágico,” a national designation recognizing towns with remarkable heritage. Stop by the church late in the day, on your way back from the basalt prisms.

Drive about twenty minutes from the entrance to Huasca to reach Peña del Aire, a viewpoint on the edge of a very deep canyon. The view extends toward the Barranca de Metztitlán Biosphere Reserve. The more adventurous cross the void on a bicycle suspended from a steel cable or on a zip line. The site opens daily at 9 a.m. On Hidalgo’s back roads, residents sometimes set up roadblocks to ask for a passage fee: France Diplomatie advises paying, as the amounts are small.

activities.text: Turquoise water, rowboats, and the smell of grilling: Bosque de las Truchas, in San Miguel Regla, is a recreation park surrounding a trout lake. You can fish with a rod rented on-site, even if you have no experience. Admission ranges from 30 to 299 pesos depending on the activities you choose, such as a rowboat ride or zip-lining. Grill your catch under the palapas, open-sided shelters set up for cookouts.

Huasca de Ocampo even has a museum dedicated to duendes, the elves of Mexican folktales: the Museo de los Duendes. A visit takes about 45 minutes and costs 40 pesos per person. It is a fun stop with children, to fit in between the basalt prisms and the village center.

days_plan.itin_title: Teotihuacán, Real del Monte, Tlaxcala, and Puebla in 7 Days

places.name: Huatulco

visits.text: Bahía San Agustín, the westernmost of Huatulco's 9 bays, is home to a coral reef. The bay is sheltered by its geography, which keeps the water calm and clear. Two beaches frame it: San Agustín and Cacalutilla. Reached partly by a dirt track, it calls for a day trip from La Crucecita and stays unspoiled on weekdays.

La Crucecita, Huatulco's urban center, sits about ten minutes from the beaches but offers all services: markets, Oaxacan cuisine restaurants, handicrafts (barro negro, mezcal, chocolate). Its central plaza is framed by colonial arcades. A good base for exploring the bays by day.

Bahía Cacaluta: this kilometer-long beach protected by an island was the filming location for Alfonso Cuarón's film Y Tu Mamá También. It backs onto dunes and remains deserted on weekdays. Accessible by a 2.5 km trail from the road, or by boat from Santa Cruz.

Boat tour of the Huatulco bays from the Santa Cruz marina: in one day, a panga visits 5 to 7 of the 9 bays. The route passes El Bufadero—a rock formation that shoots a 10 m jet of water in heavy swell—and runs along the cliffs of Huatulco National Park (119 km²). Stops at Maguey (2 hours of swimming on golden sand) and Chachacual (the wildest, reachable only by sea).
La Entrega, reachable by road from Santa Cruz (2.5 km): a wide beach with calm water and a good coral reef 50 m from the shore. Snorkelling gear for rent on site.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Bahía San Agustín: the reef spreads from shore, between the bay's rocks. Rays, sea turtles, groupers, parrotfish. Restaurants on the beach rent masks and snorkels. Water is clear enough to see the bottom at 5-6 m depth.

Diving or snorkeling during the boat tour: tour guides stop in bays where water is clearest. If you have your own equipment, save it for Bahía San Agustín or La Entrega—stops at crowded bays during daytime are sometimes brief.

Evening in La Crucecita: plaza restaurants offer Oaxacan coastal cuisine—shrimp ceviche, fish tacos, tlayudas with seafood. This is the last night on the coast: take advantage to taste local mezcal at a plaza mezcalería.

places.name: Izamal Yuc

visits.text: Completed in 1561, the San Antonio de Padua convent was built by the Spanish on Izamal’s Maya acropolis, the large platform that supported the temples. Its atrium, an immense courtyard in front of the church, ranks among the largest in the world. Diego de Landa, the fourth bishop of Yucatán, lived here. Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass here in August 1993. Visit in the late afternoon, then return in the evening for the light show.

Izamal’s biggest surprise is the Kinich Kak Moo pyramid, rising among the city streets. Its base covers about 8,000 m², more than a soccer field. The Itzamatul temple, southeast of the main square, is a reminder that the Maya city had other major buildings. Visit the pyramid in the morning, before the heat sets in, and bring water.

activities.text: This yellow is no ancient tradition: Izamal’s facades received their shared color in the late 1950s. Mayor Jorge Carlos González Rodríguez, who served from 1959 to 1961, had advertising signs removed. He also had the houses painted yellow and white. The city became a Pueblo Mágico in 2002, an official Mexican designation for towns that have preserved their character. Wander without a map through the streets around the convent toward the end of the day, when the light softens the colors.

If you are in Izamal on a Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, stay for Senderos de Luz at 8 p.m. This projection mapping show casts animated images onto the walls of the former convent. It tells the story of the Maya, the colonial era, and today’s traditions. The route starts at Parque de Los Cañones and takes about 40 minutes. Buy your ticket, priced at 163 pesos for foreign visitors, at the Palacio Municipal between 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on show days.

places.name: Jalpan de Serra Que

visits.text: Two double-headed eagles devour snakes on the facade of the Santiago de Jalpan mission. Built from 1751 to 1758 under the direction of Father Junípero Serra, it is the first of the five Franciscan missions of the Sierra Gorda. UNESCO added them together to the World Heritage List in 2003. The Pame, an Indigenous people of the sierra, were their builders. At the top of the facade, a clock installed in 1898 replaces the former statue of Saint James. Return in the late afternoon, when the ocher pilasters take on a warm hue.

You will understand the sierra better after an hour at the Museo Histórico de la Sierra Gorda, housed in a fort built in 1576 that also served as a prison. Archaeological artifacts, photographs, and everyday objects tell the region’s story. One room presents the Sierra Gorda Biosphere Reserve, established in 1997, which covers about a third of the state. It ranges in elevation from 350 to 3,100 m: this difference explains its fifteen types of vegetation, from forests to semidesert scrub. Stop here before heading to the missions.

activities.text: If you have two hours to spare, walk to Presa Jalpan, the reservoir 1.5 km from the center. Since 2004, it has been listed under the Ramsar Convention, an international agreement that protects wetlands. Pelicans, ibises, and ospreys, birds of prey that dive for fish, share the water with turtles. You can go kayaking or take a rowboat ride. Bring binoculars.

You’ll drive 40 km north on Highway 69 toward Río Verde to see the San Miguel Concá mission. It is the smallest and northernmost of the five missions, probably completed in 1754. On the facade, look for the rabbit, a Pame symbol, near the double-headed eagle and an image of the Christian Trinity. Its name is thought to come from a Pame word meaning “with me.” Allow 2 hours 30 minutes for the round trip, including the visit, and return to Jalpan before dark.

visits.text: Hundreds of long stone noses cover the facade of Codz Poop, the Palace of Masks at Kabah. Each belongs to a mask of Chaac, the Maya rain god, recognizable by his oversized nose. The site borders Route 261, less than half an hour south of Uxmal. Budget for a ticket at each site along the Ruta Puuc: Kabah, Sayil, Xlapak, and Labná charge separate admission fees.

An 18 km Maya causeway once connected Kabah to Uxmal. This sacbé, a raised road 5 m wide, was marked at each end by a monumental arch. Kabah’s arch, at one of these ends, still stands. Walk beneath its stones: you are at the start of the ancient road to Uxmal.

visits.text: Human faces in stucco, wearing headdresses and ear ornaments, flank the staircase of Kohunlich’s Temple of the Masks, built around 500 CE. They represent the city’s rulers, associated with the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, and were originally painted red. They are so well preserved because a later building covered them after 700 CE. It protected them for centuries. Get close to the masks to examine the headdresses in detail.

The name Kohunlich is not Maya: it comes from the English “Cohune Ridge,” meaning a ridge of cohune palms. Its original name remains unknown. The city, inhabited as early as 200 BCE, was designed to retain rainwater. Channels directed runoff into cisterns and an enormous reservoir. A large, elevated acropolis stands to the north. The site is 9 km south of Highway 186: stock up on water before leaving the main road.

places.name: La Paz

visits.text: On arriving in La Paz from Loreto, head to the malecón to explore the bay on foot. The promenade follows the water, offering views of the boats and waterfront sculptures. In the late afternoon, the bay changes color with the sunset. Stop for dinner in one of the waterfront restaurants before continuing your walk along the water.

La Paz's malecón stretches 5 km along the bay. At sunset, the whole town gathers here. Look for the bronze dove sculpture commemorating the rescue of Isla Espíritu Santo in the 1990s - when Mexican and American activists bought the island to prevent casino construction. The bay turns orange in minutes - take your time.
La Paz's municipal market is smaller than Tijuana's but more authentic. Catch of the day, giant gulf shrimp, aromatic herbs. Taste the machaca (shredded dried beef) at one of the adjoining fondas.

Isla Espíritu Santo is a national park and has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005. The island consists of brick-red volcanic cliffs plunging into turquoise water—no permanent infrastructure and no inhabitants. Boats leave La Paz's port for a 90-minute crossing. First stop: Los Islotes, rocky islets north of the archipelago where a colony of the gulf's California sea lions gathers—up to 800 individuals. The pups approach divers out of curiosity.

activities.text: If you still have energy after the drive, head to Playa Balandra; plan for a round trip from La Paz for this first glimpse of the gulf's waters. This enclosed bay is protected—the water is calm, transparent, and Caribbean in color. Locals come here to swim on weekends. Entry is regulated and visitor numbers are limited.

After Los Islotes, the pangas head up toward the island beaches. La Ensenada Grande, on adjacent Isla Partida, was voted one of the world's 12 most beautiful beaches by The Travel magazine. Snorkeling on the reef, kayaking in the coves, beach lunch with ceviche prepared on board. This is the trip's highlight - don't go in bad weather.

visits.text: The arch at Labná alone makes this final stop on the Ruta Puuc worthwhile. About 6 m high and 3 m wide, it retains well-preserved bas-reliefs. It was not a city gate: it served as a passage between two public spaces. Arrive before noon, as you still have a 1-hour-45-minute drive to Homún afterward.

The Palacio de Labná extends for about 120 m across two levels, making it one of the longest continuous buildings in the Puuc region. A Maya date carved into the palace corresponds to the year 862. A sacbé, a ceremonial road, connects it to the arch. Beside the arch, the Mirador is a pyramid topped by a temple. Follow this road from the palace to the arch, as the inhabitants once did.

visits.text: According to Arqueología Mexicana magazine, the Santa María del Agua de Landa mission has the finest sculpture of the five. Built from 1760 to 1768, it is the last in the series. Look at the mermaids: their faces have Indigenous features, a sign of the collaboration between missionaries and local artisans. The very narrow bell tower is integrated into the facade. In front of the church, the atrium is an enclosed, paved forecourt with a cross at its center. Landa is 20 km from Jalpan via Highway 120.

Next, you’ll take the road to Tilaco, 18 km northeast of Landa, to see the San Francisco del Valle de Tilaco mission. Built from 1754 to 1762, it is the best preserved of the five. Its facade combines four mermaids with Indigenous features, ears of corn, and cherubs. At the corners of the forecourt, the capillas posas remain: small chapels where processions would stop. The church stands on a slope, and its bell tower serves as a buttress to support it. Allow nearly 2 hours for the round trip from Landa.

A carved jaguar looks at you from the facade of Nuestra Señora de la Luz de Tancoyol, the most ornate of the five missions. It was built in the 1760s under the direction of Friar Juan Ramos de Lora. One figure has the features of the Olmecs, a very ancient civilization of Mexico. The pyramid-shaped dome of the bell tower also recalls the cultures that existed before the arrival of the Spanish. The central niche, which housed the Virgin, is empty. From Landa, drive about 5 km on Highway 120 to the turnoff, then follow 30 km of paved road.

activities.text: Bright pink, but off-limits for swimming: the pools at Las Coloradas are part of an active industrial saltworks. Their color comes from salt-loving bacteria and brine shrimp, tiny crustaceans. Strong sunlight intensifies the pink. Guided tours are available on foot, by bicycle, or in an all-terrain vehicle, daily from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. In June 2026, the walking tour cost 236 pesos per adult. Come between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m., when the pink is most pronounced.

visits.text: The San Ignacio → Loreto road swings to the peninsula's eastern side. You leave the Pacific for the Sea of Cortez—colors shift: the water turns from gray-green to deep turquoise, and the Sierra de la Giganta mountains plunge straight into the sea. Stop at the overlooks above the coast along the final 40 kilometers.

The Nuestra Señora de Loreto Conchó mission, founded on October 25, 1697, by the Jesuit Father Juan María de Salvatierra, is the first permanent mission established in the Californias—the “mother of all missions”, as the traditional expression goes. It served as the starting point for a network of 27 missions that would extend into Alta California. Today, the original church still stands in the heart of town.

Loreto's malecón is one of the peninsula's most tranquil waterfronts. A few restaurants, fishing boats, the national park islands visible a few kilometers out. Settle in late afternoon to watch the pelicans return.

Bahía de Loreto National Park protects 790 km² of the Sea of Cortez, including five uninhabited islands. Isla Coronado, 45 minutes away by boat, is the most visited: white-sand beach and water at 24°C in season. Buoys mark the snorkeling area—you will encounter groupers, parrotfish and, with a little luck, dolphins approaching the boat.

activities.text: Optional excursion: the San Javier mission, 38 km away in the mountains, is considered the most beautiful mission in Baja California. Built between 1699 and 1758, its Baroque façade of carved stone is exceptionally well preserved. Allow approximately 1 hour by road through the sierra from Loreto to reach it.

California sea lions frequent the rocks of Isla Coronado. Boat trips let you get close to them—some operators offer swimming with them in marked areas. At the end of the day, return to the malecón for a dinner of chocolate clams, the clam endemic to Loreto's waters.

visits.text: Mahahual’s malecón, the waterfront promenade, brings the whole village together: restaurants, beach clubs, and dive centers. The lighthouse and large “Mahahual” letters mark its northern end. The Costa Maya cruise port is just 3 to 5 km away, and cruise passengers come here on port days. This coast is often affected by sargassum starting in April or May. Explore the promenade on foot or by bike toward the end of the day.

activities.text: Just a few swimming strokes will get you there: in Mahahual, the coral reef begins a few meters from the beach. It is part of the Mesoamerican Reef, the barrier reef along the Caribbean coast. It breaks the waves, keeping the water on the beach side calm and shallow, suitable for snorkeling. Rent equipment from a waterfront dive center. Do not touch or stand on the coral: it is very fragile.

visits.text: The cobbled streets of Mapimí smell of dry dust and old wood. This Pueblo Mágico, founded in 1598 around the Ojuela mines, was once one of the richest mining towns in the north. The Templo de Santiago Apóstol, with its carved cantera façade, overlooks the main square. Its Callejón de las Flores still carries the memory of the years of the Revolution.

The Panteón Municipal de Mapimí is not a must-see, and yet it deserves 20 minutes. Sculptor Benigno Montoya carved angels in cantera of unexpected delicacy for a desert village cemetery. Look for the 17th-century colonial tombs at the back of the plot.

Built in 1898 by Roebling's Sons Company of New York—the firm behind the Brooklyn Bridge—the Puente de Ojuela spans an 80-meter-deep canyon over a 318-meter length. It linked the Ojuela mine to the mining camp. Declared a national monument since 1984.

activities.text: Visit the Museo Benito Juárez in the Recinto Hidalgo: it was in this house that Hidalgo, Allende, Aldama, and Jiménez stopped four days before their execution in Chihuahua. The interior is austere but the story chilling. Usually free entry, check hours on arrival.

Under your feet, the wooden planks of the Puente de Ojuela creak with each step and the canyon opens 80 meters below. The crossing takes ten minutes, no more. On the Ojuela side, visit the tunnels of the Mina Santa Rita with a local guide: inside, a mummified mule in an alcove will stop everyone dead.

visits.text: The Durango → Mazatlán road is one of North America's most spectacular highway stretches. Highway 40D, inaugurated in 2013, crosses the Sierra Madre Occidental with 115 bridges and 61 tunnels. The most striking: Puente Baluarte, a 1,124-meter-long cable-stayed bridge whose roadway is 403 meters above the canyon floor—the highest road bridge in the Americas. You cross in 60 seconds what took 4 years to build.

Mazatlán has an old center—Olas Altas and Plazuela Machado—that bears no resemblance to the hotel zone. 19th-century theaters, pastel colonial façades, fresh fish markets. Plazuela Machado is the city's most beautiful square: palm trees, central fountain, bandstand, and restaurants with outdoor terraces.

The Teatro Ángela Peralta, inaugurated in 1874, is old Mazatlán's architectural jewel. Its neoclassical façade and 841-seat hall were completely restored in the 1990s. If a performance is scheduled during your visit, get a ticket—the acoustics are exceptional.

Climb up to Cerro del Vigía, the hill overlooking the old center. It's the former lookout post where sailors signaled arriving ships. Today: panoramic views over the bay, Venados and Chivos islands offshore, and the Pacific stretching to the horizon. Remarkable sunset.

activities.text: Mazatlán's malecón stretches 21 km—the longest in the world according to locals. Rent a bike in late afternoon and ride along the Pacific coast until sunset. Pacífico, the local beer brewed in the city since 1900, is drunk cold on the old center's terraces.

The Pino Suárez fish market is the best place for lunch in Mazatlán. Fishermen deliver in the morning—marlins, tunas, giant shrimp, oysters. The fondas around the market serve ceviches and aguachiles prepared to order. This is also where you'll find the best marlin tacos.

places.name: Mazunte

visits.text: From Puerto Escondido, the road hugs the coast eastward for 75 km—an hour and a half of switchbacks between cliffs and tropical vegetation. Mazunte appears at the end of a sandy track. Three streets, a few bars, a beach. Drop your bags and head straight into the water.

Playa Mazunte, a kilometer-long strip of golden sand with turquoise waters. Waves are moderate on the east side, calmer near the rocks to the southwest. Late afternoon, fishermen return with their catches. No striped beach chairs, no vendors—just the beach.

The Centro Mexicano de la Tortuga is one of Mexico's most active sea turtle conservation centers. It protects olive ridley, black, hawksbill, and leatherback turtles—from nesting (July to January) to release. You'll see the animals in their different developmental stages. For decades, Mazunte was Mexico's turtle hunting center; the creation of the center in 1991 radically changed the community's relationship with these animals.

Punta Cometa, the southernmost promontory of Oaxaca state, is the best sunset spot on the Oaxacan Pacific coast. The path from Mazunte beach climbs 15 to 20 minutes on a rocky trail. At the end, rocks plunge into the Pacific with a 180° view. Locals call this place “Cerro Sagrado”—sacred hill—and it was already used as an astronomical observatory in pre-Hispanic times. Arrive 45 minutes before sunset to find a good rock.

Playa Rinconcito, a 10-minute walk from central Mazunte, is the quietest of the village's three beaches. A few palapa restaurants under coconut palms, few people even in high season. The current is strong to the west—swimming on the east side only.

Zipolite, 3 km from Mazunte by collectivo, is Mexico's most famous nude beach. The beach runs for 1.5 km and receives powerful waves—among the country's most dangerous due to strong currents. Swimming is not recommended outside marked areas. But the roots atmosphere, bars on stilts, ocean views in late afternoon: all this explains why travelers planned for 3 days stay 3 weeks.

activities.text: Arrival and settling in. For those with energy after the drive, a short walk on the Punta Cometa trail in late afternoon. Otherwise, first sunset from the beach with a mezcal bought at the village shop.

Swimming and marine wildlife observation at San Agustinillo, 1.2 km from Mazunte on foot. This 1,300 m beach naturally divides into two parts: west side protected by rocks, gentle waves, ideal for swimming; east side, stronger swells for bodysurfing. From December to March, whale families sometimes swim in the bay.
Snorkeling at Playa Estacahuite, 1 km from Puerto Ángel on a dirt road. A healthy coral reef, accessible from shore. Calm water, varied fauna. A few palapas and food stands on the beach.

Free beach day and yoga: several venues offer early morning classes on Mazunte or San Agustinillo beach. The Oaxacan coast has attracted a community of practitioners since the 2000s. Ask your accommodation for daily schedules.
