places.name: Mérida

visits.text: Chichén Itzá early in the morning—tour buses arrive after 10am, so be there at 8am. The Pyramid of Kukulcán stands 30 meters tall with four staircases of 91 steps each: 364 total, plus the temple platform, equals 365—one for each day of the year. During the spring and autumn equinoxes, the shadow of the corners draws the undulating body of a serpent descending toward the carved head at the base of the stairs.

Izamal, 1.5 hours' drive toward Mérida, is the yellow city of Yucatán: all colonial buildings are painted ochre gold, in the colors of the Vatican flag. The Franciscan Convent of San Antonio de Padua (1561) was built on the ruins of the Mayan pyramid Pap-Hol-Chac—its 7,806-square-meter atrium is the second largest in the world after St. Peter's Square. Pope John Paul II celebrated mass here in 1993.

Mérida's historic center centers on the Zócalo and its cathedral (1598), built largely with stones from a demolished Mayan pyramid. The adjoining government palace houses large murals tracing the history of Yucatán.

Paseo de Montejo, a boulevard lined with oleanders and bordered by 19th-century hacienda palaces, is Yucatán's answer to the Champs-Élysées. The Palacio Cantón, one of the avenue's finest buildings, houses the Regional Museum of Anthropology—a perfect introduction to Mayan civilization before visiting the sites.

Uxmal, 80 kilometers from Mérida, is one of the most beautiful sites in Yucatán and far less crowded than Chichén Itzá. The Pyramid of the Magician (28 meters) is the only Mayan pyramid with an elliptical floor plan. Its facade is entirely covered with masks of Chaac, the rain god—hundreds of hooked noses stacked for several meters. The Nunnery Quadrangle below is a masterpiece of geometric mosaic.

Kabáh, 20 kilometers south of Uxmal on the Puuc route, features the Codz Poop: an entire facade covered with 250 Chaac masks, overlapping from ground to summit. It's one of the most densely decorated facades in all Mayan architecture.

activities.text: Climb the Kinich Kakmó pyramid in Izamal—34 meters high, one of the largest pyramids in Yucatán. Panoramic views over the golden city below. Access is free and it's rarely crowded.
Drive to Mérida in late afternoon—1.5 hours from Izamal. Settle in for the night in the capital of Yucatán.

Lucas de Gálvez market for lunch—Mérida's largest covered market. Try sopa de lima (lemon broth with crispy tortillas and shredded chicken), panuchos, and papadzules. The steam from cochinita pibil will guide you to the right stalls.

On Sunday, head to Plaza Grande in the historic center for Mérida en Domingo: stalls selling crafts and Yucatecan food around the square, with musical performances and dancing. Browse the stalls, then sit facing the cathedral to watch life on the square.
The Uxmal sound and light show happens every evening at dusk—colorful projections illuminate the temples and Chaac masks. A spectacle that transforms the site. Ask about showtimes at the entrance.

Puuc route by car: between Uxmal and Kabáh, several smaller sites follow in sequence—Sayil, Labná (with its Mayan triumphal arch), Xlapak. Few crowds, plenty of character. Worth doing at your own pace if you have a car.

visits.text: Plaza Grande helps you get your bearings in Mérida: the four main buildings in the city center surround it. The government palace stands on the north side, the cathedral on the east, Casa de Montejo on the south, and the municipal palace on the west. The Spanish founded the city on January 6, 1542, on the site of a Maya city called T’hó. Make this square your first stop, early in the morning before the midday heat.

Construction of San Ildefonso Cathedral began in 1561, using stones taken from the pyramids of T’hó, the Maya city on which Mérida was built. Its first phase of construction ended in 1598. It is the oldest cathedral in the Americas, excluding the Caribbean islands. Enter from Plaza Grande and avoid Mass times so you can walk around without disturbing worshippers.

Step inside the Palacio de Gobierno, on the north side of Plaza Grande, to see the murals by painter Fernando Castro Pacheco. They tell the history of Yucatán through a series of large scenes. The building still houses the Yucatán state government: you are visiting a workplace, not a museum. Allow 45 minutes to view the paintings in sequence, and keep your voice down near the offices.

Casa de Montejo is worth a stop, especially since admission is free. This house on the south side of Plaza Grande was the residence of Francisco de Montejo, known as “el Adelantado.” This title designated the conquistador commissioned by the king of Spain to conquer a region. It is the oldest house in Yucatán, now converted into a house museum. It opens at 10 a.m.: save it for late morning, after the cathedral.

Save the Gran Museo del Mundo Maya for last: it puts everything you have seen along the way into context. The museum, in northern Mérida, takes you through three galleries: the Maya of today, the Maya of yesterday, and the ancient Maya. Allow about 2 hours for the permanent exhibition. It is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and closed on Tuesdays; general admission costs 200 pesos, and parking is free.

activities.text: If you enjoy beautiful facades, walk along Paseo de Montejo in the late afternoon. This broad avenue in Mérida is lined with grand early 20th-century homes and sculptures. These houses reflect the city’s wealth at the time. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the walk and bring water, then take a taxi back to the center if the heat feels oppressive.

visits.text: The people of Monclova call it “la Capital del Acero”: AHMSA, the integrated steelworks of the Altos Hornos de México group, is based here. But before the steel there was the colonial town: the Parroquia de Santiago Apóstol, completed in the seventeenth century in sillar stone, still carries bullet marks from the Revolution on its façade. Worth a quick look if you are in transit towards Monterrey.

places.name: Monte Albán Oax

visits.text: To build Monte Albán, the Zapotecs leveled a mountaintop 400 m above the Oaxaca Valley. Their capital was founded around 500 B.C. At its peak, it had about 35,000 inhabitants. On the 300 m central plaza, look for the Danzantes gallery. These carved stones depict naked men in contorted poses, perhaps captured enemy leaders. The site is open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last entry at 4 p.m., and admission costs 210 pesos for foreign visitors. Arrive at opening time with water and a hat.

This is not a temple: Monte Albán’s Edificio J served as an astronomical observatory, along with neighboring Edificio P. At its base, “conquest stones” show the symbol of Monte Albán and an upside-down head representing a defeated enemy. Each commemorates a victory won between 100 B.C. and A.D. 200. Next, head to the large ball court, where players struck the ball with their hips, elbows, and knees. Finish at the steps of the Plataforma Norte, once the elite’s residential quarter.

Save the Museo de sitio de Monte Albán for last. This small site museum is included in your admission ticket. Its exhibits focus on original carved stones. After visiting the ruins, you will recognize the Danzantes and the glyphs, the written symbols carved into the stone. Allow 30 minutes.

visits.text: The Macroplaza plays in the big leagues of the world's great plazas with its 40 hectares—and yet it never overwhelms. The Faro del Comercio, a 70-meter orange tower designed by Luis Barragán, projects a green laser beam across the city every night. Arrive before 9am to see the square without crowds, and take time to walk along the north side of the Metropolitan Cathedral, with its pink baroque facade.

The cobblestones of Barrio Antiguo smell of roasted coffee and fresh paint. This quarter, founded in the 17th century and rebuilt in the 18th, is now Monterrey's densest zone of galleries and bars. On Sunday mornings, a flea market takes over Calle Morelos—arrive early, vendors pack up by noon.

When the Compañía Fundidora de Fierro y Acero went bankrupt in 1986, Monterrey converted its 144 hectares of blast furnaces into Parque Fundidora, Mexico's largest industrial archaeology site. The Museo del Acero Horno3 is housed inside blast furnace #3, still standing. Park entry is free; the museum charges a separate ticket.

Ride the Paseo Santa Lucía by boat from Parque Fundidora to the Macroplaza: 2.5 km of artificial canal inaugurated in 2007, designed to link the park to the historic center without a car. The ride takes about 35 minutes. Perfect for ending the day with your feet up.

The Cerro del Obispado and its Museo Regional are worth the final climb: from this promontory above Monterrey, the Sierra Madre Oriental frames the city in a single view. The museum traces the history of Nuevo León from colonial times. Open Tue-Sun, 9am-6pm.

activities.text: If you start at Parque Fundidora early in the morning, you can rent bikes for free Tuesday through Sunday. Loop the park in an hour before the weekend families arrive, then continue on foot to Barrio Antiguo, 15 minutes away.

Here, the evening meal goes by the name cabrito—whole kid goat roasted over embers—or machacado, dried beef shredded with eggs. This isn't Mexico City cuisine. Grab a table in Barrio Antiguo, which comes alive after 8pm, and stay for a live show at Café Iguana if it's a weekend.

End the trip by walking the Paseo Santa Lucía from the Macroplaza to Parque Fundidora: 2.5 km of canal along gardens, sculptures, and terrace restaurants. Free, open all day. Perfect for a final lunch before heading to the airport.

places.name: Morelia

visits.text: Morelia Cathedral began in 1660 and finished in the 18th century—a baroque-neoclassical blend built entirely in local pink stone. Two 64-meter towers dominate Plaza de Armas. The domes are covered in azulejos. Saturday evenings, a sound-and-light show projects onto the facade.

Morelia's aqueduct has 253 arches spanning 1,700 meters, built 1705–1730 to channel water from nearby springs. It's superbly illuminated at night. Calzada Fray Antonio de San Miguel runs alongside—a tree-lined pedestrian promenade leading to the Sanctuary of Guadalupe, whose gilded, colorful interior is visually stunning.

Palacio de Gobierno, facing the cathedral, merits a detour for Alfredo Zalce's interior murals. They trace Michoacán's history from the Purépecha through Independence. The Conservatory of Las Rosas, founded 1595, is one of the Americas' oldest music schools—its children's choir is renowned throughout Mexico.

Palacio Clavijero is a former 17th-century Jesuit college with an impressive baroque octagonal dome. It now hosts quality temporary exhibitions and is free to visit. Just next door: the candy street—dozens of shops selling dulces de Morelia, goat-milk candies and candied fruits specific to Michoacán.

Pátzcuaro (1 hour from Morelia) is a pueblo mágico built on a lake at 2,000 meters elevation. Plaza Vasco de Quiroga is one of Mexico's largest colonial plazas—200 meters long, ringed by white arcades, centered by a statue of the 16th-century bishop who protected the Purépecha from slavery.

The boat crossing to Janitzio (30 minutes) traverses Lago de Pátzcuaro. From the dock, you see the island crowned by the giant statue of Morelos, Independence hero, fist raised. The Purépecha consider this lake the gateway to the underworld—Día de Muertos ceremonies here on November 1st are among Mexico's most authentic.

The famous butterfly nets of Purépecha fishermen—shaped like monarch butterfly wings—have become Janitzio and the lake's symbol. Today they're mostly used for tourist photos and demonstrations, commercial fishing having evolved. But the spectacle remains beautiful, especially early morning from the dock.

In Pátzcuaro, Casa de los Once Patios is a former 18th-century Dominican construction with eleven interior courtyards. It now houses artisan workshops: golden lacquerware, ceramics, hammered copper from Santa Clara, Purépecha embroidery. It's Michoacán's best place to buy authentic handicrafts directly from artisans.

activities.text: Evening stroll along the illuminated aqueduct, then drinks on a downtown bar terrace. Morelia is lively at night—studious, relaxed, and local. It's a city that often surprises travelers who weren't expecting it.

Excursion to Tzintzuntzan on the way back (15 minutes from Pátzcuaro). It was the capital of the Purépecha empire before the conquest—it held out against the Aztecs in the 15th century, notably thanks to its mastery of copper. Five terraced pyramids (the yacatas) overlook the lake. Admission fee.

Pátzcuaro's artisan market around Plaza Gertrudis Bocanegra. The former church converted into a library houses at the back a monumental fresco on Michoacán's history—often overlooked by guides, very beautiful.

visits.text: Cobalt blue walls and a yellow kitchen: the Casa Azul (Blue House), now the Museo Frida Kahlo, has preserved the painter’s colors. Frida Kahlo was born here in 1907 and died here in 1954. In the studio, her wheelchair faces an unfinished portrait of Stalin. Above her bed, a mirror attached beneath the canopy helped her paint her self-portraits. The museum has no ticket booth: buy your ticket online (320 pesos) before visiting. Closed on Mondays. The ticket also includes admission to the Diego Rivera-Anahuacalli Museum.

visits.text: The Museo Nacional de Antropología makes an impression as soon as you enter the courtyard: an enormous roof, nicknamed “el Paraguas,” the umbrella, rests on a single column. Opened in 1964, the museum has 23 exhibition halls devoted to Mexico’s cultures. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. In 2026, admission costs 210 pesos for foreign visitors. Arrive at 9 a.m. and choose a few halls, as seeing everything in one morning is difficult. The nearest subway station is Auditorio, on Line 7.

Often called the “Aztec calendar,” the Piedra del Sol is not a calendar. Archaeologists believe it was more likely a ceremonial basin or sacrificial altar. This stone disk measures 3.6 m in diameter and weighs nearly 25 tonnes. It was found beneath the Zócalo in 1790, while the square was being paved. It then remained mounted on a cathedral tower until 1885. Originally, it was painted blue, red, green, and yellow. See it first, before the groups arrive.

places.name: Oaxaca City

visits.text: The Zócalo is the essential starting point. Around this central plaza—a UNESCO World Heritage site—stand the 16th-century Catedral Metropolitana and the Palacio de Gobierno with Arturo García Bustos's murals narrating the entire history of the state. Set down your coffee and watch: this is where the city breathes.

The Mercado 20 de Noviembre, built in 1862, is the sanctuary of Oaxacan cuisine. Step into the Pasillo de Humo—that smoke-filled corridor where dozens of vendors grill tasajo (thinly sliced beef), chorizo, and cecina over charcoal asadores. Choose your meat at the counter, sit at the stone tables, and wait. An experience worth the journey on its own.

The Andador Turístico, a pedestrian street connecting the Zócalo to the Templo de Santo Domingo. In the evening, musicians play at the terraces, painters exhibit on the sidewalks. It's the living axis of the colonial city, to be explored without any particular destination in mind.

Monte Albán opens at 8am—be there at opening. The morning light is perfect on the Gran Plaza, a 300 m by 150 m esplanade perched 400 meters above the central valleys. This Zapotec capital founded around 500 BC once had up to 40,000 inhabitants spread over 20 km². Allow 2.5 hours for the visit. The site is 10 km from Oaxaca, a 20-minute drive.

The Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán features one of Mexico's most impressive Baroque facades. Construction began in 1572 and lasted over a century. Inside, gilded stucco covers the nave from floor to ceiling. Don't miss the Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca in the adjoining former convent: it displays the 600 pieces of Mixtec treasure discovered in Monte Albán's Tomb 7 in 1932—jewelry in gold, jade, and turquoise.

The Jalatlaco barrio, east of the centro, is a well-preserved neighborhood of the colonial city. Its cobbled lanes, its houses with ochre and pink façades, its bougainvillea spilling over the walls: this is where artists and photographers set up their tripods. Look out for the murals that bring the walls to life.

San Bartolo Coyotepec lies 11 km south of Oaxaca. This village of 600 families produces barro negro, a glossy black pottery. The current technique dates back to the 1950s, when Doña Rosa Real discovered that by polishing the still-damp clay with a quartz stone before firing, it came out a deep metallic black. Step into the family workshops to see the hand wheel and the firing in a closed kiln that starves the clay of oxygen.

Santo Tomás Jalieza, a few kilometers away, specializes in backstrap loom weaving, a pre-Hispanic technique where the weaver attaches the loom to their own waist and uses their body tension to keep the threads taut. Village women produce belts, bags, and blouses with geometric Zapotec patterns.

If you're there on a Friday, don't miss the Ocotlán de Morelos market: one of the most authentic in the central valleys. Wool blankets, medicinal herbs, dried meats, ceramics—vendors arrive from surrounding villages before dawn.

Cuajimoloyas, 2 hours by mountain road from Oaxaca, is the most accessible village of the Pueblos Mancomunados. It sits at over 2,700 m elevation. In summer, the undergrowth overflows with edible mushrooms. In winter, the cloud forest wraps century-old pines in perfect silence. This is where the Sierra Norte opens up to hikers.

Benito Juárez, a pioneer village of Zapotec community ecotourism, features a spectacular suspension bridge and viewpoints overlooking the central valleys. On clear days, you can spot the Oaxaca plain 2,400 m below. The communities manage the cabañas with fireplaces, the meals, and the guides themselves.

Hierve el Agua, 70 km east of Oaxaca, is one of Mexico's strangest geological formations. Springs saturated with calcium carbonate have deposited their minerals for millennia, creating two petrified waterfalls that overlook the valley from a cliff over 200 m high. The large waterfall measures 60 m high by 90 m wide. Natural pools allow for swimming. The view from the cliff edge is breathtaking.

Mitla, on the return route: this 14th-century Zapotec archaeological site is famous for its stone mosaic fretwork—geometric patterns assembled without mortar that entirely cover palace facades. Unique in Mesoamerica. The Spanish built a red church right in the middle of the site, reusing Zapotec stones.

Teotitlán del Valle, 30 minutes from Oaxaca, is the world capital of Zapotec rugs. In family workshops, weavers work on large pedal looms introduced by the Spanish in 1535. Wools are dyed with cochineal (nopal cactus insect, which gives red), indigo (blue), walnut shell (brown), and cempasúchil flower (yellow). A quality rug can take several weeks.

activities.text: Chocolate de agua session at the market: Oaxacan chocolate is prepared with water (not milk), ground on-site with cinnamon and sugar. The molinos at the market let you choose your proportions. Order a hot jícara with pan de yema—egg yolk brioche, a local specialty.

First glass of mezcal at a vineta in the centro: Oaxacan mezcal comes from wild agaves—espadín, tobalá, tepeztate—distilled in artisanal palenques. Ask for a young mezcal (joven) for your first taste. It's different from tequila: smokier, more complex.

Walk through the Jardín Etnobotánico de Oaxaca, adjacent to the Santo Domingo convent: two hectares of giant cacti, agaves, and medicinal plants used by indigenous cultures for centuries. Guided tour only—essential to understand what grows here.

Mezcal tasting in Santiago Matatlán, dubbed the world mezcal capital. The mezcal route passes through this village where over a hundred artisanal producers (palenques) distill their agaves in clay stills. Ask to visit an active palenque: you'll see agave piñas cooking in earth pits, distillation in wooden vats, and taste different expressions of espadín and cuishe.

Trek or mountain bike between Cuajimoloyas and Benito Juárez on marked trails (red for main routes). Over 100 km of trails cross the 8 mancomunados villages. The path between these two villages follows pine and oak forests, passes a 30 m waterfall, and offers 180° views of the Sierra Madre. Local guides available for Spanish-language accompaniment.
Zipline and suspension bridge at Cuajimoloyas: the communities have built a 1 km zipline and suspension bridge over a forested canyon. An option for those wanting adrenaline between hikes.

Swimming in Hierve el Agua's natural pools: the water ranges between 22 and 27°C, rich in minerals, pleasant especially from March to June. A loop trail (45 min) descends to the foot of the waterfalls for a different angle. Bring good shoes—the altitude makes the climb harder than it appears.

visits.text: The gilded interior of the Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, Oaxaca’s grand Dominican church, catches your eye as soon as you enter. More than 60,000 sheets of 23.5-karat gold leaf were used to decorate the interior. Just past the entrance, look up: the ceiling depicts the family tree of Saint Dominic, the order’s founder. From 1866 to 1902, the church and neighboring convent served as barracks. The church reopened for worship in 1938, and the convent became a museum. Be discreet during Mass.

The Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca occupies the former Santo Domingo convent. Gallery III displays the treasure from Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, discovered by archaeologist Alfonso Caso on January 9, 1932. Exhibits include gold jewelry, rock crystal cups, and a skull covered in a turquoise mosaic. These objects are Mixtec: the Mixtecs reused the tomb long after the Zapotecs, the people who founded the city. Allow 2 hours for the 14 galleries. Admission costs 210 pesos for foreign visitors.

Walk up Andador Macedonio Alcalá, the pedestrian street in downtown Oaxaca. It is paved with cantera verde, a green stone also found on many of the city’s monuments. Closed to cars since 1985, it runs through the historic center, which was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987. The center follows a grid layout, with square blocks measuring about 100 m on each side. Notice the thick walls and low facades: the city lies in an earthquake zone, and buildings were kept low to withstand tremors. Walk along the street in the morning, before the heat sets in.

With free admission, the Museo Textil de Oaxaca offers the best introduction to the textiles you will later see in the villages. It brings together nearly 6,000 pieces from six private collections: cloth, towels, and clothing from several regions and periods. The museum also offers weaving workshops using a backstrap loom, whose threads are held taut by a strap worn around the waist. Registration is required for these workshops. A free guided tour in Spanish is offered on Wednesdays at 5 p.m.

Three successive cathedrals have stood on the edge of Oaxaca’s Zócalo, the central square laid out in 1529. The first two were destroyed by earthquakes, in the 16th and then the 18th century. Construction of the current Catedral de Oaxaca began in 1702, and it was consecrated in 1733. Its facade is made of green stone. Inside, the neoclassical decor, inspired by ancient Greece and Rome, is more restrained. Afterward, sit near the Zócalo’s bandstand, installed in the early 20th century, and watch life unfold in the square.

After the tombs of Monte Albán, the Museo de Arte Prehispánico Rufino Tamayo offers another perspective: that of a painter and collector. In 1974, Rufino Tamayo donated his collection and the 18th-century house that holds it to Oaxaca. It displays more than 1,150 pieces from Mesoamerica, the name given to the ancient civilizations of Mexico and Central America. Save it for the end of your stay: you will recognize styles you have seen during the trip.

Cerro del Fortín hosts the Guelaguetza on the two Mondays following July 16. If the first falls on July 18, the celebrations are postponed by a week, to July 25 and August 1. During this festival, troupes from the eight regions of the state of Oaxaca dance in costume, accompanied by their brass bands. The word comes from the Zapotec language and means “to cooperate.” Performances take place in the Auditorio Guelaguetza, an open-air venue with tiered seating for 11,400. During the rest of the year, head up in daylight for the view of the city center and Juárez’s motto, carved in stone letters on the hillside.

The reddish stone facade of the Basílica de la Soledad is sculpted like an open folding screen. Father Fernando Méndez had this Baroque church built in the late 17th century. Take time to look at the facade from the forecourt, then enter quietly outside service times.

activities.text: If you enjoy gardens that tell the story of a culture, set aside 1 hour for the Jardín Etnobotánico de Oaxaca. Ethnobotany studies the relationships between peoples and the plants they use. The garden occupies the former grounds of the Santo Domingo convent, which served as barracks from the mid-19th century until 1994. Since 1998, it has brought together hundreds of species from every region of the state. Visits are in groups with a guide. Confirm the schedule at the garden’s reception desk the day before.

The smell of grilled meat leads you to the pasillo de humo, the “smoke corridor” at Mercado 20 de Noviembre. The process is simple: choose raw meat, tasajo (beef) or chorizo, and it goes straight onto charcoal grills. Other stalls sell tortillas, vegetables, and drinks, and diners eat at shared tables. Construction of the market began in 1862. It is open daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Try one of the moles, too: these are thick, chile-based sauces.

Continue to Mercado Benito Juárez, one block south of the Zócalo, for flowers, fruit, sorbets, hats, leather goods, and knives. Around the markets, vendors sell chapulines, grasshoppers fried with chile. Also look for tejate, a cold drink made with corn, cacao flowers, and the seed of mamey, a tropical fruit. If you get hungry again, order a tlayuda: a large, crisp corn tortilla topped with grilled beef, cheese, and avocado.

visits.text: Painter Rodolfo Morales never forgot his hometown, Ocotlán de Morelos. In 1992, he established a foundation that restored the former Dominican convent, founded in 1555 and abandoned in 1885. The convent now houses a museum featuring works by Morales, crafts from Oaxaca, and colonial-era art. The neighboring church, also restored, is still used for worship. Allow 1 hour for the museum and church.

activities.text: If you visit on a Friday, set aside the morning for the tianguis in Ocotlán de Morelos, its weekly market. It is one of the oldest and largest in the Central Valleys, the valleys surrounding Oaxaca. Residents of neighboring villages sell their farm products, everyday items, and crafts here, including textiles from Santo Tomás Jalieza. Schedule this day for a Friday if you can.

Take a detour to Santo Tomás Jalieza, a neighboring village nicknamed “the village of belts.” Embroidered belts in fabric or leather are sold here. The same patterns appear on clothing, bags, and pouches. It is a good place to buy a lightweight gift to tuck into your suitcase. Compare several stalls before choosing, as the finish varies from piece to piece.

visits.text: Art Nouveau outside, Art Deco inside: the Palacio de Bellas Artes changed styles during construction. Begun in 1904 with plant-inspired curves, it was completed in 1934 with geometric lines. Like the cathedral, it is sinking into the soft ground: about 4 m since 1904. Its Diego Rivera mural, “Man, Controller of the Universe,” was originally intended for Rockefeller Center in New York. It was destroyed there because the Rockefellers objected to its depiction of Lenin. Rivera recreated it here in 1934. Museum admission is free on Sundays.

visits.text: If you secure a spot, the grand staircase of the Palacio Nacional tells the history of Mexico through Diego Rivera’s paintings. Between 1929 and 1935, he covered three walls: on the right, the world before the Spanish arrived; in the center, the conquest, independence, and the Revolution; on the left, the 20th century, featuring Karl Marx. The palace occupies the site of the residences of the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II. The guided tour is free, but spots are scarce, and tours may be canceled without notice. Arrive early at the Ministry of Finance museum on Moneda Street with identification.

visits.text: Misol-Ha is a 35-meter waterfall cascading into a natural pool surrounded by tropical vegetation—you can walk behind the falls on a small path. Ideal stop to break up the long drive from Campeche. 20 kilometers from Palenque.

The Roberto Barrios waterfalls, reached by car from Palenque, are less well known than Misol-Ha but often more beautiful depending on the season: successive falls, pools for swimming and the turquoise water of Chiapas rivers. Some local operators offer guided swimming trips.

The Temple of the Inscriptions is Palenque's main pyramid—22 meters high, with 617 Mayan glyphs on its walls. In 1952, archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier discovered a secret stairway descending into the heart of the pyramid: the tomb of King Pakal, who died in 683 after a 68-year reign. His 13-tonne sarcophagus is still there.

The Royal Palace is a labyrinthine complex of courtyards, corridors, and chambers stacked on a 100-by-80-meter platform. Its four-story tower served as an astronomical observatory—the only tower of its kind in Mayan architecture. The wall reliefs recount military victories and court rituals under Pakal's reign.

activities.text: Drive from Campeche to Palenque (about 6 hours). Long leg, but the landscape changes dramatically: from the Yucatán plain to the first forested mountains of Chiapas. Evening arrival in Palenque, dinner in town.

Evening stroll through downtown Palenque—a small, lively town with no pretensions, good Chiapan taquerías, and an active zócalo. The howler monkeys you'll hear tomorrow morning are already part of the soundscape.
Arrive when the site opens (8am). Howler monkeys start calling at dawn—a deep, primal sound rising from the jungle below the temples. It's one of Mexico's most powerful auditory memories.

Alberto Ruz Lhuillier Museum, included with site admission: 200 pieces recovered from Palenque, including a scale reproduction of Pakal's tomb with its famous jade mask. Don't miss the Otolum waterfalls in the park before heading to the museum—cold, clear water.

visits.text: Founded in 1597 with authorization from King Felipe II, Casa Madero is the oldest winery on the American continent. The hacienda—which locals simply call "Casa Grande"—still produces wine and brandy in century-old cellars. The guided tour lasts about 1.5 hours and includes a tasting.

The Capilla del Santo Madero on its hill is worth the walk up: from the heights of Sombreretillo, you embrace Parras and its vineyards planted in the Coahuilan desert in a single view. The climb takes 20 minutes from the center. Bring water.

Stroll through Parras's centro histórico and look for the Casa donde nació Francisco I. Madero, future Mexican president and figure of the Revolution. The town dates from 1598 and its colonial streets house the Alameda 20 de Noviembre, several old churches, and the Museo del Vino.

activities.text: In the cellars of Casa Madero, the coolness contrasts with the desert heat outside. The classic tasting covers their red wines: Shiraz, Merlot, and Cabernet Sauvignon. The '3' wine is often cited by travelers as their favorite. Book the bodega visit in advance on the official website.

In August, if your timing coincides with the Feria de la Uva de Parras, the entire village celebrates the grape harvest with parades, horse races, and evening concerts. The rest of the year, the Sunday market at Plaza del Reloj is enough to capture the atmosphere.

places.name: Pinal de Amoles Que

activities.text: The dirt road is bumpy, but the Cuatro Palos viewpoint is worth every jolt. At around 2,700 m, this viewpoint is 12 km from Pinal de Amoles, a 30-minute drive up a steep dirt road. The marked trail is 2.3 km long with 125 m of elevation gain, about a 50-minute walk. At the top, temperate forests stretch to the east and semidesert scrubland to the west. On a clear day, you can see the Peña de Bernal. At dawn, a sea of mist fills the valleys.

visits.text: Oaxaca → Puebla drive (about 5 hours). Puebla is a major colonial city at the foot of the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes—the first two things visible on approach. Afternoon arrival and first exploration of the UNESCO-listed historic center, entirely cobbled and pedestrian.

Barrio de los Sapos is Puebla's quarter of antique dealers and artisans—facades covered with talavera ceramics, small galleries, pulque bars. Puebla talavera has been inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2019; authentic pieces bear an official seal.

The Capilla del Rosario in the Church of Santo Domingo is nicknamed 'the eighth wonder of the world'—a side chapel entirely covered in gold leaf, sculpted stucco, and talavera tile from floor to ceiling. Built between 1650 and 1690, it's the finest example of churrigueresque baroque in Mexico. Free admission, and the effect is immediate.

The Biblioteca Palafoxiana is the oldest public library in the Americas (1646), inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Its 17th-century cedar shelves still hold 45,000 volumes including 15th-century incunabula. A visit takes less than an hour.

activities.text: Puebla dinner: mole poblano was born here in the 17th century in a convent—a sauce with 20 ingredients including cacao, dried chiles, and spices. Chalupas (oval tortillas topped with beans and salsa) are the emblematic street food. El Parián market sells them all day.

Evening visit to Museo Amparo—one of Mexico's best private pre-Columbian museums, with a collection of Mayan, Aztec, and Zapotec pieces displayed in a beautifully restored colonial space. Open until 6pm.
Mole tasting in a covered market—Mercado de la Victoria or El Parián market have comedores (small family eateries) where mole negro has been simmering since morning. Eat at the counter with locals.
Walk through the historic center—Puebla has more than 70 religious buildings in its center alone, and its Baroque façades covered in talavera ceramics are characteristic of the city.

visits.text: Seventy meters: that is the height of the Catedral de Puebla’s two towers, the tallest in Spain’s American colonies at the time. Bishop Juan de Palafox y Mendoza consecrated the cathedral on April 18, 1649, before it was even finished. Legend has it that angels hoisted its great bell, María, which weighs more than 8 tonnes. In reality, Juan Bautista Santiago, an Indigenous master builder, raised it in 1732. Dress appropriately: this is an active church.

Gold all the way up to the dome: the Capilla del Rosario, in the church of Santo Domingo, is covered in gilded stucco. This is a sculpted plaster coating covered with 24-karat gold leaf. The chapel was consecrated in 1690, when the friar Diego de Gorozpe dubbed it “the eighth wonder of the world.” Talavera tiles cover the lower walls. It is located at 407 Avenida 5 de Mayo; visit outside service times.

Poblanos, the residents of Puebla, named the Casa del Alfeñique after a sweet. Alfeñique is a sugar-and-almond paste, and the house’s facade is covered with mortar ornaments so delicate that they resemble this decorative sugar work. The house was built for Juan Ignacio Morales, a master ironworker. It later became home to the city’s first public museum, which displays more than 1,500 historical objects. Allow 45 minutes.

It is Puebla’s most impressive room: the Biblioteca Palafoxiana, a vaulted gallery 43 m long, completed in 1773. It all began in 1646, when Bishop Juan de Palafox y Mendoza donated 5,000 books to a college on the condition that everyone could read them. UNESCO recognizes it as the first public library in the Americas. Admission costs 48 pesos and is free on Sundays; the library opens at 10 a.m., Tuesday through Sunday.

If you could visit only one museum in Puebla, choose the Museo Amparo. It occupies two colonial mansions from the 17th and 18th centuries and has fourteen exhibition rooms. The displays take you from objects made before the Spanish arrived to colonial-era furniture, then contemporary art. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes so you do not have to rush.

Step inside the Uriarte workshop, which has been making talavera, Puebla’s painted earthenware, since 1824. This earthenware takes its name from Talavera de la Reina, the Spanish town that gave this pottery its style. Everything is handmade, and a single piece can take up to three months of work. Each object bears a serial number, and most are signed by the artisan. Ask at the front desk whether a workshop tour is scheduled that day.

On May 5, 1862, around the Fuertes de Loreto y Guadalupe, General Ignacio Zaragoza’s Mexican army defeated the French troops led by the Count of Lorencez. This was the Battle of Puebla. At Fort Loreto, the Museo de la No Intervención occupies the former chapel, among other spaces, and displays cannons, sabers, and documents from the battle. The forts are in the Centro Cívico 5 de Mayo, outside the historic center: take a taxi.

activities.text: Next, stroll through the mercado de El Parián, Puebla’s handicraft market, within walking distance of the main square. Most stalls are permanent, while other vendors display their goods on blankets spread on the ground. Compare prices before buying. For certified talavera, choose an established workshop such as Uriarte, whose pieces bear serial numbers.

Puebla residents say mole poblano originated in a convent. According to the story, the nuns of Santa Rosa, anxious about an archbishop’s upcoming visit, mixed chili peppers, spices, and chocolate, then poured the sauce over an old turkey. Other accounts trace it back to the Aztecs, but there is no evidence that they added chocolate. Try mole at lunch, then save room for a cemita, a large sandwich piled with fillings and served on a round sesame seed roll.

places.name: Puerto Escondido

visits.text: The descent from Oaxaca to the coast (via San José del Pacífico) takes 6 to 7 hours on tight switchbacks through the Sierra Madre del Sur. The landscape changes dramatically—cloud forest, then tropical, then the first ocean scents. Puerto Escondido appears by late afternoon. Drop your bags and head down to see Zicatela before dinner.

Playa Zicatela is one of the world's most renowned surf breaks: the Mexican Pipeline generates hollow tubes of 3 to 6 meters breaking over shallow sand. For non-surfers, settle on the beach with a coconut juice and watch: it's a spectacle in itself. Don't swim—the currents and wave power are deadly for untrained swimmers.

Playa Carrizalillo, west of Puerto Escondido, is the local swimming beach. A protected cove accessible by a 167-step stairway from the cliff. Calm water, gentle waves, clean sand. Vendors offer kayak and paddleboard rentals.

The Mercado Benito Juárez of Puerto Escondido is the local market, far from tourist circuits. Vegetables, tropical fruits, medicinal herbs, handmade huaraches. A good hour to understand what the people of the Oaxacan coast actually eat.

Parque Nacional Lagunas de Chacahua, created in 1937, protects 14,175 hectares of coastal lagoons, mangroves, dunes, and tropical forests between Puerto Escondido and Santiago Jamiltepec. From the village of Zapotalito (1.5 hours by road), a lancha crosses the two large lagoons—Pastoría and Chacahua—through mangrove tunnels. On the banks: white egrets, iguanas, American crocodiles sunning themselves.

Playa Chacahua, accessible only by boat: a long strip of white, deserted sand facing the open Pacific. A few palapas serve grilled fish. The waves roll gently—ideal for bodysurfing. The kind of place you talk about for years afterward.

activities.text: Surf lesson at La Punta: this stretch of beach at the western end of Zicatela receives gentler, more consistent waves—perfect for beginners. Local instructors offer 2-hour sessions including equipment and instruction. La Punta is also Puerto Escondido's most laid-back neighborhood, with its small fish restaurants and hammocks.

Nighttime bioluminescence tour at Laguna de Manialtepec, 18 km west of Puerto Escondido. This 15 km coastal lagoon harbors microscopic plankton that glows blue-green with the slightest movement. On new moon nights, every gesture in the water triggers a luminous trail. Providers organize kayak or boat outings, followed by a swim in the glowing water under the stars. Book ahead—spots are limited to about ten people per group.

Daytime kayak through Manialtepec mangrove: morning outings navigate tunnels of red mangroves, where egrets, frigatebirds, ibises, and storks nest. Ornithologist guides count over 150 observable species. Another way to discover the same lagoon, in completely different light and atmosphere.

Visit the Cocodrilario de Chacahua: this breeding center houses over 200 American crocodiles of all sizes, from hatchlings to 2 m adults. The program aims to reintroduce the species into the lagoons, where it had nearly disappeared in the 1970s due to poaching.

Bird watching during the lancha crossing. The park harbors over 150 species, including the roseate spoonbill (Platalea ajaja) with spectacular pink plumage, brown pelican, magnificent frigatebird, and migrating storks. Ask the pilot to slow down in narrow channels.

places.name: Puerto Vallarta

visits.text: Puerto Vallarta's Malecón is a 1,300-meter promenade facing Banderas Bay. No cars—only pedestrians, palm trees, and every 100 meters a bronze sculpture. The collection brings together fifteen works by Mexican artists installed since 1960. Most famous: 'La Rotonda del Mar,' eight monumental thrones resembling a Tim Burton scene. At the end, the Voladores de Papantla perform several times daily—they descend spiraling from a 30-meter pole hanging by their feet.

Zona Romántica, also called Old Town or Viejo Vallarta, is the historic district south of the Cuale River. Cobblestone streets, white houses with red-tiled roofs, wrought-iron balconies overflowing with bougainvillea. This is where locals eat, where neighborhood bars and the best street food concentrate—lime ceviche, shrimp tacos, churros.

Iglesia Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, with its distinctive crowned dome, is Puerto Vallarta's symbol visible from everywhere. Built early 20th century, the bell tower was damaged in a 1995 earthquake—the crown was remade in stone-covered concrete. Nighttime processions pass the church almost nightly during the Virgen de Guadalupe festivities in December.

Yelapa is a boat-access-only village 30 km south of Puerto Vallarta, at the back of a cove surrounded by dense jungle. No cars here—you move on foot or by donkey. The beach is uncrowded, fish come straight off fishermen's boats. Water taxis leave from Playa Los Muertos all morning.

Isla Cuale (Isla del Río Cuale) is a small river island in downtown Puerto Vallarta, accessible via pedestrian bridges. It hosts hidden restaurants, a handicraft market, an archaeological museum, and a village atmosphere apart from the Malecón's bustle.

activities.text: Sunset from Playa Los Muertos. Puerto Vallarta's best-known beach faces directly onto the Pacific. The Los Muertos pier spirals out into the sea—it's the best spot to watch the sun disappear into the water with no obstacles. Beach bars serve margaritas and cold beer with feet in the sand.

Dinner in Zona Romántica. It's the circuit's finest gastronomic evening. Pescado zarandeado (fish marinated and charcoal-grilled, served on banana leaves), raicilla (local mountain agave spirit, rustier than tequila), and lime-marinated seafood. Small street restaurants are worth as much as white-tablecloth establishments.

Alternative to Yelapa: boat excursion in Banderas Bay to the hidden southern beaches—Las Ánimas, Quimixto. Tour operators offer outings with snorkeling in rocky coves. December through March, humpback whales come to calve in the bay—seeing them breach is common on these trips.

Final waterfront evening on the Malecón. The sculptures shift appearance under streetlight glow. Promenade restaurants serve until midnight. The Pacific, at this hour, makes its waves heard beneath the conversations.

visits.text: Querétaro's aqueduct delivers the first visual punch upon arrival. Built between 1726 and 1738 by Marquis Juan Antonio de Urrutia y Arana—local legend claims he built it to bring water to a nun he loved. Seventy-four pink stone arches stretch 1,280 meters long and rise 23 meters high. It still feeds the downtown fountains today.

Plaza de Armas anchors the UNESCO-listed historic center (inscribed 1996). Surrounding it: the 18th-century Palacio de Gobierno, arcades sheltering terrace restaurants, and at the center a fountain honoring the marquis who built the aqueduct. It's one of Mexico's best-preserved colonial plazas—not a fast-food joint in sight.

The Templo de la Cruz sits on a hill at the edge of the historic center. From there, at the Los Arcos mirador, you get the best view of the aqueduct, especially late in the day when the pink stone turns golden.

Jardín Zenea is where Queretanos come to pause. A central kiosk, benches beneath giant ficus trees, cafés spilling onto sidewalks. Querétaro consistently ranks as Mexico's most livable city—streets are clean, crime is low, the atmosphere peaceful.

activities.text: After dark, the historic center transforms. Storytellers lead nocturnal walking tours through the alleys recounting city legends—Inquisition ghosts, Emperor Maximilian's execution at Cerro de las Campanas in 1867. Surprisingly well-done and hugely popular with Mexican families.

Querétaro's gastronomy deserves a stop at Mercado de la Cruz, a few blocks behind the center. Ground-floor fondas serve enchiladas queretanas, pozole, and tamales for next to nothing. This is where locals eat.

places.name: Real de Catorce

visits.text: Real de Catorce exists only because silver was abundant here. At its peak around 1890, the town counted 40,000 inhabitants. When silver prices collapsed after 1900, only 1,500 remained. Today the cobblestone streets are half-deserted, colonial façades crumbling. That's the charm: a town frozen in time. The parish church of the Purísima Concepción in the town center dates from the 18th century—its baroque altars and 19th-century pipe organ are still in place.

To enter Real de Catorce, you pass through the Ogarrio tunnel—2.3 km carved through rock in 1901, hewn from an old mine passage, lit with yellow light, and one-way. You wait your turn at the entrance. When the gatekeeper opens the barrier, you enter the darkness. It's the best decompression chamber ever invented.

activities.text: Descend into the Wirikuta desert by Willys jeep or on horseback with a local guide. This is the sacred land of the Wixárika (Huichol) people, who make a pilgrimage here every spring from Nayarit—several hundred kilometers—to harvest peyote as part of shamanic ceremonies. On rocks and bushes, you'll see offerings of colored wool shaped like diamonds—nierika, portals between worlds. Don't touch them. The sacred mountain Cerro El Quemado dominates the desert.

places.name: Real del Monte Hid

visits.text: Four hundred meters of mine passage dug into the mountain: that is the route through the Mina de Acosta in Real del Monte, whose official name is Mineral del Monte. This silver mine operated from 1727 to 1985. It is now a museum, where you walk through the tunnel in the miners’ footsteps. Bring a sweater: the town sits at an elevation of 2,712 m. Ask locally about tour times.

The most surprising place in Real del Monte is a cemetery: the Panteón Inglés, the English Cemetery, which opened in 1851. Its 755 graves are arranged in rows facing England, the homeland of the miners who came to work here. Only one grave is an exception, and tradition attributes it to the English clown Richard Bell. Walk slowly along the paths: at this elevation, even the slightest climb leaves you breathless.

The south tower of the Parroquia de Nuestra Señora del Rosario has a clock added in 1842 thanks to donations from miners. At the time, many of these workers came from England: the first English technicians had arrived in Mexico in 1824. Most came from Cornwall, a mining region in southwestern England. Begin your visit to downtown Real del Monte in the church square, then stroll through the neighboring streets.

If you are interested in the miners’ history, step inside the Museo de Medicina Laboral, the museum of occupational medicine. It is housed in the Centro Cultural Nicolás Zavala. The town had its own miners’ hospital as early as 1907, funded jointly by the workers and the Compañía Real del Monte y Pachuca, the company that operated the mines. Allow 40 minutes and visit it on the same day as the Mina de Acosta.

In Real del Monte, the local specialty is called a “paste”: it is the Mexican cousin of the pasty, the savory turnover eaten by Cornish miners. The Museo del Paste, which opened in 2012, explains how this potato and ground meat turnover arrived with the English miners. Those same miners also brought soccer to the region. Visit the museum in the late morning, just before heading out to try a paste.

activities.text: Try a piping-hot paste at a shop in downtown Real del Monte: it is the easiest lunch of the day. The original recipe combines potatoes and ground meat in pastry folded into a turnover. Pick up a second one for the drive to Huasca de Ocampo, about 20 minutes away.

visits.text: “Estero de los Lagartos,” the inlet of the lizards: this is what the sailors of Spanish explorer Francisco Hernández named this place in 1517. They were looking for fresh water. The many “lizards” they saw were actually crocodiles. Crocodiles still live in the reserve. The small port of Río Lagartos has kept that name. Stroll along the lagoon toward the end of the day, on your way back from Las Coloradas.

activities.text: Explore Ría Lagartos, a long saltwater lagoon lined with mangroves, by boat with a local guide. This biosphere reserve covers more than 60,000 hectares and protects the American flamingo and two crocodile species. As many as 77,000 flamingos have been counted along this coast, where most of the region’s breeding pairs nest. Set out around 7 a.m., when the light is soft and the heat bearable. Ask the boat operator to turn off the engine and keep a distance from the birds.

visits.text: Four pavilions, a T. rex skeleton, and rain every 14 minutes: Saltillo's Museo del Desierto, inaugurated in November 1999, is one of the most comprehensive natural history museums in the north of the country. In the outdoor patio, the downpour lasts 45 seconds—kids love it, adults too. Closed Mondays.

The Catedral de Santiago de Saltillo deserves a stop even for non-believers: its pink quartzite facade dating from the mid-18th century blends baroque and neoclassical with a mastery quite rare in northern Mexico. It houses the Santo Cristo de Saltillo, one of Coahuila's most venerated religious images.

The Coahuila sarape is woven in colors that exist nowhere else in Mexico—sulfur yellow, chili pepper red, electric blue. The Museo del Sarape y Trajes Mexicanos in the centro histórico presents weaving techniques and exhibits historical pieces. Allow 45 minutes to walk through.

activities.text: Walk the centro histórico on foot from the Cathedral to the Plaza de Armas, then continue to Parque Mirador for a view of the Cathedral and the Sierra Madre Oriental. The round trip takes a leisurely hour. Take the opportunity to have lunch at a fonda in the center: Coahuilan cuisine follows much the same style as Nuevo León's.

places.name: San Bartolo Coyotepec Oax

visits.text: The Museo Estatal de Arte Popular de Oaxaca, which opened in 2004 in San Bartolo Coyotepec, provides an overview of the valleys’ crafts in just a few galleries. The first displays the finest examples of barro negro, the village’s black pottery. Another brings together wood carvings from San Martín Tilcajete, mostly masks. Visit before heading to the workshops: you will be better able to recognize a carefully crafted piece.

activities.text: Barro negro has not always been black. For most of its history, pottery from San Bartolo Coyotepec was gray with a matte finish. In the 1950s, potter Doña Rosa Real discovered that polishing nearly dry clay before firing gave the finished piece a glossy black finish, without paint. Her family still works in the home’s workshop, around the courtyard. Pack your purchases carefully: these decorative pieces are fragile.

places.name: San Cristóbal de las Casas

visits.text: In the historic center of San Cristóbal de las Casas, head to the Templo de Santo Domingo. Its pink Baroque façade is covered in carved reliefs. In front of the church, the craft market stalls display Tzotzil textiles. Continue on foot toward the Zócalo to explore the center's colonial streets.

San Cristóbal de las Casas sits at 2,200 meters elevation—the air is cool, the light different, the atmosphere radically more mountainous and indigenous. The colonial center around the Zócalo and Templo de Santo Domingo contrasts sharply with the jungle left behind that morning. The colorful huipils of Tzotzil women at the market are an immediate visual shock.

San Juan Chamula, 10 kilometers from San Cristóbal, is a Tzotzil village entirely autonomous from the Mexican government—it has its own laws and police. The Church of San Juan Bautista is Chiapas' most fascinating place: no pews, the floor covered with pine needles and hundreds of candles. Shamans perform healing rituals with eggs, soda, and herbs. Photos strictly forbidden inside—and the ban is serious.

The amber market on Real de Guadalupe is one of Mexico's best-stocked: Chiapas is one of the world's major amber producers. Pieces containing fossilized insects or plants are the rarest. Learn to distinguish real amber (it floats in salt water) from plastic imitations.

Sumidero Canyon: 30 km of vertical cliffs reaching up to 1,000 meters high, carved by the Grijalva River. Drive from San Cristóbal to Chiapa de Corzo to board the boat. The boat trip downstream from Chiapa de Corzo takes around 2 hours and passes caves, waterfalls, and osprey nests. Crocodiles bask on the banks—keep an eye on the water.

Chiapa de Corzo, reached by car from San Cristóbal, is a small colonial town on the Grijalva and the starting point for canyon excursions. The hexagonal fountain in Plaza Central (1562) is the town's emblem—Mudéjar style, red brick, the only example of this style in the Americas. Allow 30 minutes to visit.

activities.text: Walk around the Zócalo in San Cristóbal de las Casas and look at the colonial façades and arcades bordering the square. Then walk to the Templo de Santo Domingo to examine the carved motifs on its façade and browse the craft stalls set up in front of the church.

Evening on Andador Real de Guadalupe—San Cristóbal's pedestrian street, lined with cafés, bookstores, mezcal bars, and Tzotzil boutiques. Chiapas coffee, grown at altitude, is among Mexico's best. Take time to savor a cup.

San Cristóbal's craft market around Templo de Santo Domingo—Tzotzil textiles, Lacandon pottery, painted wooden figurines from Zinacantán. Women in black wool dresses with colored threads sell their wares directly on the forecourt.
Tasting pox (pronounced 'posh')—the ceremonial corn liquor of the Tzotzils, not to be confused with mezcal. Several bars on Real de Guadalupe offer pox-based cocktails. An unusual local experience.

Evening stroll in San Cristóbal—the city changes after 6pm. Markets empty, cafés fill, and colonial lantern light gives the Baroque facades a warm glow. The night market on Calle 20 de Noviembre serves Chiapan quesadillas and tamales.

Mezcal bar on Real de Guadalupe for your last evening in San Cristóbal. Chiapas mezcals (made from wild agave) are less famous than Oaxaca's but often wilder. Bartenders at the good establishments explain the differences between espadín, tobalá, and cuishe.

places.name: San Ignacio

visits.text: In San Ignacio, explore the oasis on foot around the central plaza. The San Ignacio Kadakaamán mission borders this shaded square: examine its stone façade, then step inside the church. The nearby streets offer views of the date palms surrounding the village. Return to the plaza for a break in one of the restaurants around the bandstand before continuing to explore San Ignacio.

The Jesuit mission of San Ignacio Kadakaamán was founded in 1728. It's one of the best-preserved in all of Baja California - its black volcanic stone facade and baroque bell tower stand on the palm-shaded plaza. It served as a base for missionaries reaching the Cochimí communities in the surrounding mountains. Step inside: the acoustics are remarkable and the original ornaments are still in place.

Explore the oasis of San Ignacio from the streets around the central plaza. The palm grove contrasts with the desert landscapes crossed on the road: date palms, fig trees and orange trees fill this hollow in the peninsula. On foot, view the gardens from public streets and look at the façades of the village houses. Return to the San Ignacio Kadakaamán mission to examine the details of its stone façade, then take a break in the shade on the plaza, near the bandstand and restaurants.

activities.text: In the afternoon, set off for San Ignacio (about 2 hours). After hours of flat desert, the San Ignacio oasis looks as though it has landed in the wrong landscape: 80,000 date palms, fig trees, and orange trees clustered in a hollow in the peninsula. Settle in on a terrace on the central plaza to unwind after the day.

In the evening, join the locals on the plaza of San Ignacio. It's one of the few plazas on the peninsula still lively in the evening—a few restaurants around the central bandstand, kids on bikes. The contrast with the hours spent crossing the desert is complete.

places.name: San José del Cabo

visits.text: San José del Cabo has an authentic colonial center—no nonstop partying, no noise: cobbled lanes, an 18th-century church, contemporary Mexican art galleries in converted colonial houses. Thursday evenings, the “Art Walk” brings together about twenty galleries open simultaneously from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. (October to June). It's the calm, cultured version of Los Cabos.

30 km from San José, Cabo San Lucas is at the other end of the spectrum: a packed marina, bustling beaches, seaside bars. El Arco—two rocks sculpted by erosion at the junction of the Pacific and the Gulf of California—can be visited by panga from the marina. Playa del Amor, accessible only by boat, lies just behind. The Pacific water is cold, the gulf water lukewarm—you feel the difference just 10 meters apart.

Final morning in Los Cabos. If your flight is in the afternoon, you still have a few hours. Return to El Médano beach for a final swim; plan for a round trip from San José del Cabo. Or browse the market in San José del Cabo to take home a few specialties: Baja California black salt, Valle de Guadalupe wines, and local pottery.

activities.text: Final dinner in Los Cabos: the food scene is strong—seafood tacos at San José's marina and chef-led waterfront restaurants in Cabo San Lucas. Enjoy the sunset from El Médano, Cabo's main beach; plan for a round trip from San José del Cabo.

Los Cabos International Airport (SJD) is 20 minutes from downtown San José del Cabo. Return the vehicle early - drop-off formalities can take time depending on the rental company. Allow 2 hours before the flight.

places.name: San Luis Potosí

visits.text: San Luis Potosí's Plaza de Armas is over 430 years old—it's the heart of the historic center. Surrounding it: the baroque cathedral built between 1670 and 1730, with its pink cantera stone façade and sculptures of the twelve apostles carved in Carrara marble, and the Palacio de Gobierno, where Benito Juárez established his government in 1863 during the French occupation. Take time to sit on the plaza benches in late afternoon.

The Jardín de San Francisco is the city center's second major garden. The adjacent baroque church houses a remarkable sacristy and colonial paintings. Right next door, the Museo Regional Potosino occupies a former convent—its Aranzazú chapel on the second floor is one of the most elaborately decorated baroque spaces in the city.

The Teatro de la Paz, inaugurated in 1894, is one of Mexico's most beautiful neoclassical theaters. Its gray cantera façade is worth a detour even if you are not attending a performance. Step into the lobby if it is open—the ceiling frescoes have been restored.

activities.text: Enchiladas potosinas are San Luis's unmissable specialty. Unlike enchiladas you might know, these are red corn tortillas (chile ancho worked into the dough) stuffed with fresh cheese and fried, served with cream and salsa. They bear no resemblance to Tex-Mex versions. Look for a cocina económica around the Mercado de la República—that's where they're at their best.

activities.text: It is hard to leave San Martín Tilcajete empty-handed, with its streets lined with alebrije workshops. These are imaginary animals carved and then painted in bright colors. Pedro Linares, an artisan from the Mexico City area, dreamed up these creatures after a high fever in the 1930s and gave them this name. Here, they are carved from copal, a local wood that has become scarce. The carver roughs out the shape with a machete, then refines it with a knife. Visit two or three workshops to compare styles before buying.

places.name: San Miguel de Allende

visits.text: Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel dominates the main plaza with its pink neo-Gothic spires. What most don't know: a self-taught 19th-century mason named Zeferino Gutiérrez redesigned the facade inspired by a postcard of Cologne Cathedral—without ever leaving Mexico. The result is magnificent oddity, improbable tropical Gothic.

San Miguel counts over 150 art galleries—a rare concentration for a city of 175,000. Fábrica La Aurora, a former 1902 textile mill converted into a cultural center, gathers 40 studios and galleries under one roof. Original stone arches and machinery create an unlikely backdrop for contemporary sculptures and abstract paintings.

The UNESCO-listed historic center is compact and entirely pedestrian. Cobblestone streets like Calle Cuna de Allende, with coral and ochre facades, frame direct views to the Parroquia's spires. The town hosts about 10% foreign expats—the vibe is cosmopolitan but not artificial: local markets and neighborhood festivals coexist with gourmet restaurants.

activities.text: Climb to Mirador El Chorro late afternoon. The trail starts from Parque Juárez—you'll pass the 18th-century washbasins, still in use. From the lookout, the entire town unfolds backlit: the Parroquia's bell towers, red-tiled roofs, golden hills. It's the circuit's finest sunset.

Wander San Antonio and Guadalupe streets for street art. Over 100 murals cover walls in the peripheral neighborhoods—local and international works, some enormous. The annual Muros en Blanco festival transforms the district every year.

visits.text: Above San Pedro Garza García, the Parque Ecológico Chipinque is part of the Cumbres de Monterrey National Park. Its name comes from the Nahuatl 'chipinqui'. Coatis, white-tailed deer and red-tailed hawks cross paths with walkers on the well-marked trails. There is an entrance fee, and a light jacket is worth taking.

activities.text: Take the Brecha del Chile trail to Puerto del Aire for a 360° view of the Sierra Madre and Monterrey's metro area. The climb takes about 1.5 hours, the descent via La Florida 1 hour. Mountain bikes are allowed on Brecha del Chile only, not on La Florida.

On the ridges of Chipinque, the pine and oak forest gives way to a natural viewpoint from which Monterrey disappears into the heat haze. Two abandoned mines and the ruins of General Juan Andreu Almazán's house dot the route—few visitors pay them any attention.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeast Mexico: Monterrey, Desert & Mapimí, 14 days

places.name: San Quintín

visits.text: Between Ensenada and San Quintín, the road changes character dramatically. The carpet of vineyards gives way to agricultural plains, then desert. Candelabra cacti gradually appear. Take a break in the expanses of sand and coastal dunes north of San Quintín—the contrast with the Atlantic is striking.

The bay of San Quintín is a shallow lagoon renowned for its oyster farming. Local oystermen have worked here for decades. As you approach the water's edge, you'll see oyster beds aligned in the bay. Buy directly on-site - San Quintín's Pacific oysters have a pronounced briny taste.

activities.text: San Quintín is a transition stop—a quiet day before the major crossing of the central desert. Take the opportunity to drive along the Pacific coast at sunset: the wild beaches north of town are deserted and windswept. A few hours to catch your breath before tomorrow's 5-hour drive.

map_keywords: Bahía de San Quintín Baja California

visits.text: The Templo de Santa Catarina is visible from afar, even from the road leading to Santa Catarina Lachatao. Built of green stone between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church borders a narrow square. The Museo Comunitario de Lachatao, a small museum run by the village, occupies the same square. Lachatao belongs to the Pueblos Mancomunados, eight mountain villages that work together to welcome hikers. Stop first at the ecotourism office: it provides trail information and rents bikes, tents, and flashlights.

activities.text: Grass covers the terraces and building foundations at the summit of Cerro del Jaguar, about 2 km from central Lachatao. This archaeological site has remained almost intact. Each year, ceremonies mark the equinoxes, the two days when day and night are the same length. Hike up with a local guide and sturdy shoes.

Less than a kilometer as the crow flies separates Lachatao from San Miguel Amatlán, another village in the Pueblos Mancomunados. Amatlán offers guided tours of its mine. The village also maintains interpretive trails, paths lined with explanatory signs. You can rent bikes and buy local handicrafts there. Bring a jacket and closed-toe shoes.

If you are interested in birds, take the trail connecting Lachatao to Santa María Yavesía. It passes through a pine and oak forest. In Yavesía, a path leads down to the river and a natural waterfall. The village also organizes nature conservation workshops. Ask how long the route takes at the Lachatao ecotourism office before setting out.

In Lachatao, the dish people will recommend is chichilo de guajolote. It is a black mole, a thick chile-based sauce, served with turkey. Try it at the community restaurant next to the Templo de Santa Catarina. The village has neither a bank nor an ATM: bring enough cash for your meal, guide, and mine tour.

days_plan.itin_title: Oaxaca in 6 Days: Monte Albán, Valleys, and Sierra Norte

activities.text: Ten minutes from Ocotlán, Santa Catarina Minas distills its mezcal, Oaxaca’s agave spirit, in a distinctive way: twice, in earthenware pots called ollas de barro. This process is called “minero,” after the village’s name. Several palenques, small artisanal distilleries, explain the production process, from the agave field to the tasting. Afterward, you will need to drive 42 km back to Oaxaca: choose a designated driver who will not drink, or come with a guide.

days_plan.itin_title: Oaxaca in 6 Days: Monte Albán, Valleys, and Sierra Norte

visits.text: Not an inch is left undecorated: inside the church of Santa María Tonantzintla, stucco and paintings cover the walls, vaults, and dome. You can see cherubs, children adorned with feathers, angels with Indigenous faces, and tropical fruits such as coconuts, chili peppers, and mangoes. The name, in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, roughly means “place of our little mother.” This is the village church: enter quietly.

Perhaps the most colorful facade in the area belongs to the church of San Francisco Acatepec. It is covered in blue, yellow, black, green, orange, and purple talavera tiles interspersed with red brick. All this ceramic work was handmade. The exact construction date is unknown, but a painting in the church is signed and dated 1730. The two villages are neighbors: visit the two churches one after the other.

days_plan.itin_title: Teotihuacán, Real del Monte, Tlaxcala, and Puebla in 7 Days

visits.text: Santiago surprises: 30 minutes from Monterrey, this Pueblo Mágico declared in 2006 has kept its cobbled streets, 18th-century casonas, and its own pace. The Iglesia de Santiago Apóstol looks onto a Plaza Principal surrounded by galleries and regional restaurants—cabrito and pan de elote leading the menu.

Climb to the mirador behind the Museo de Historia de Santiago: you take in the Sierra Madre Oriental, the historic center, and the Presa de la Boca in a single glance. The museum itself—installed in the old Palacio Municipal—tells the village's past; better to visit it before climbing to the viewpoint.

A dam, in a Pueblo Mágico? The Presa Rodrigo Gómez (called Presa de la Boca) has become the village's central attraction. The view from the water's edge with the mountains in the background is worth the detour. Kayak and catamaran rentals operate in season.

The water falls in a fan over 25 meters, exactly like a horse's tail—hence the name. The Cascada Cola de Caballo, in Cumbres de Monterrey National Park, is reached by a short, accessible paved trail with several viewpoints along the way. Paid entry; arrive before 11am to avoid the weekend rush.

activities.text: If the Presa de la Boca is calm, rent a kayak instead of a motorized lancha: you hug the shores beneath the mountains without engine noise. Figure about 80-100 MXN per hour depending on the on-site renters. Avoid July weekends when the water is swarming with jet-skis.

The zip line at Parque Cola de Caballo is clearly the most fun of the side activities: the Roller Zip flies over the canyon above the waterfall. The Hacienda Cola de Caballo hotel-park also offers bungee jumping from 70 meters for those with strong stomachs. Reservations recommended on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeast Mexico: Monterrey, Desert & Mapimí, 14 days

places.name: Santiago de Querétaro Que

visits.text: Querétaro’s aqueduct stretches for 1,280 m, with 74 arches reaching up to 28 m high. The Marquis Juan Antonio de Urrutia y Arana paid for most of its construction. Thanks to him, spring water reached the city in 1735. For an overall view, head to the viewpoint in front of the Panteón de los Queretanos Ilustres, the cemetery honoring the city’s prominent figures. Josefa Ortiz de Domínguez, a figure in the independence movement, is buried there. Come late in the day, when the low-angle light picks out each arch.

Locals call it el árbol de las cruces, the tree of crosses: in the garden of the Santa Cruz convent, its thorns grow in the shape of little crosses. Legend has it that the missionary Antonio Margil de Jesús planted his walking stick here. Completed in 1683, the convent housed the first college in the Americas dedicated to training missionaries. In 1867, Maximilian of Habsburg, Emperor of Mexico, was held here for two days after his surrender. The tour takes you through the kitchen, refectory, and Maximilian’s cell: allow 1 hour.

In September 1810, the Casa de la Corregidora, on the Plaza de Armas, served as a prison for Josefa Ortiz de Domínguez. She was nicknamed La Corregidora because she was the wife of the corregidor, the magistrate who represented the king of Spain. Despite being locked up, she managed to have word sent to the priest Miguel Hidalgo that the independence conspiracy had been discovered. In the center of the square, the Marqués fountain has a local nickname: the fountain of the dogs. Walk around the square before heading to San Francisco Church.

In our view, the Museo Regional offers the best introduction to Querétaro. It occupies the former San Francisco convent, founded in 1550. Its galleries present the region’s archaeology and Indigenous peoples. On the neighboring church’s neoclassical facade, a relief depicts Saint James, Santiago in Spanish: he is the saint who gives Santiago de Querétaro its name. Inside, look for the choir loft and its carved stalls. Allow 45 minutes to 1 hour.

The gold of six large altarpieces immediately catches your eye in the Templo de Santa Rosa de Viterbo. These altarpieces, carved and gilded decorations placed behind the altars, date from the 18th century. Outside, look at the botareles, massive buttresses that support the walls. The decoration also shows a Mudéjar influence, a style that emerged in Spain from a blend of Islamic and Christian art. A school now occupies the former cloister. Allow 30 minutes.

The Templo de Santa Clara in Querétaro has lost its convent but retains its altarpieces, pulpit, and two choirs with Baroque decoration. The church was built in the early 17th century. Right next door, in the Santa Clara garden, the Fuente de Neptuno is more than 200 years old. Allow yourself this final half hour in downtown Santiago de Querétaro before heading to the airport or bus station.

visits.text: The first building you will see is the Gran Palacio de Sayil, about 85 m long. Its two stacked terraces create the illusion of a three-story building. Around the year 900, the city had nearly 10,000 inhabitants. Archaeologists estimated this figure by counting houses and chultuns, cisterns dug to store rainwater. Save some energy for the Mirador, a ruined temple 350 m south of the palace.

If time allows, stop at Xlapak, about 5 km from Sayil on the road to Labná. This unassuming site rounds out the Ruta Puuc, the route linking the Maya cities of the Puuc region: Kabah, Sayil, Xlapak, and Labná. It is a short stop but requires a separate ticket: decide when you get there, depending on how tired you feel and how hot it is.

days_plan.itin_title: Yucatán in 6 Days: Mérida, Uxmal, Izamal, and Celestún

visits.text: Sayulita, a designated pueblo mágico of 5,000 residents, sits 40 km north of Puerto Vallarta. People who knew Puerto Vallarta before it became a major resort say Sayulita resembles what it was in the '70s. Colorful cobblestone alleys, Huichol art galleries, hammocks everywhere, dogs sleeping on grocery store thresholds.

San Pancho (San Francisco) sits 7 km north of Sayulita—even quieter, even less touristy. A wide exposed beach, few restaurants, lots of locals. If Sayulita feels too busy, San Pancho is your refuge. The two connect easily by taxi or on foot along the coast.

The Islas Marietas are a national biosphere reserve off the Bay of Banderas. The two main islands, Isla Larga and Isla Redonda, are protected—no building is allowed. The surrounding waters are exceptionally clear, with 10 meters of visibility. You can spot blue-footed boobies, frigatebirds, dolphins, and humpback whales from December to March.

Playa de los Muertos, 15–20 minutes on foot from Sayulita's central square—follow the beach to the left, then climb a path behind the cemetery—is much quieter than the main beach. Good for snorkeling, rarely crowded.

activities.text: First Pacific immersion at Sayulita beach. The main beach splits in two around a rocky outcrop—one side for surfers and lessons, the other a calmer zone. Waves are gentle for beginners December through April. Surf schools offer daily lessons.

Climb Cerro del Mono in the late afternoon—the trail starts in the village of Higuera Blanca, reached by car or bus from Sayulita. Allow 1 hour for the climb, 350 meters of altitude. From the summit, a 360° view over the whole Bay of Banderas, Punta Mita, the Islas Marietas offshore, and the sunset over the Pacific. The sky turns orange and violet with nothing in the way on the horizon.

Free beach day in Sayulita if the Marietas excursion isn't possible. Surf lessons on the main beach—instructors are there from 8 AM. Grilled fish on the waterfront, shrimp ceviche, and marlin tacos are the reference dishes of the Nayarit coast.
Sunset from the main beach with a drink. The Pacific faces due west—Sayulita sunsets rank among the finest on the Mexican coast. Colors often last 30–40 minutes after the sun disappears.
