visits.text: On February 21, 1978, electric utility workers struck a stone disk more than 3.25 m in diameter. This disk, depicting Coyolxauhqui, goddess of the Moon, is the centerpiece of the Templo Mayor museum. This great temple of the Mexica, the Aztec people, honored Huitzilopochtli, god of war, and Tláloc, god of rain. It was rebuilt six times, each temple covering the previous one: as you explore the site, you walk alongside these successive temples. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the entrance on Seminario Street.

days_plan.itin_title: Mexico City in 3 Days: Zócalo, Frida Kahlo, and Xochimilco

visits.text: At least four tonnes: that is how much each serpent head projecting from the facade of the Templo de la Serpiente Emplumada, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, in Teotihuacán’s Ciudadela weighs. These heads, surrounded by feathered collars, alternate with geometric figures with round eyes. The temple dates to around 150 AD. The Ciudadela, a square enclosure measuring 400 m on each side, was not a fortress, despite its Spanish name meaning “citadel.” Arrive when it opens at 8 a.m., before the heat sets in.

Nothing prepares you for the sheer bulk of the Pirámide del Sol: 65 m tall, with a base measuring approximately 225 m on each side. The city had been abandoned for centuries when the Aztecs gave it the name Teotihuacán, often translated as “the place where the gods gathered.” Climbing is not permitted: walk around the base instead to appreciate its size. Bring a hat and water, as shade is scarce at the site.

Tools, cooking pottery, religious objects: the Museo de la Cultura Teotihuacana displays more than 600 pieces in eight galleries. They illustrate life in a city whose estimated population ranged from 85,000 to more than 150,000. Its heyday was around 250 to 550 AD. Plan to visit this museum in the middle of the day: its galleries offer a break from the sun.

If you enjoy painting, set aside 1 hour for the Museo de Murales Teotihuacanos Beatriz de la Fuente. Its nine galleries bring together murals discovered over a century of excavations, along with objects made of stone, ceramic, and obsidian, a black volcanic glass. The museum follows the site’s opening hours, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. General admission costs 210 pesos; on Sundays, admission is free for Mexican citizens and residents with proof of status.

activities.text: Next, walk along the Calzada de los Muertos, the Avenue of the Dead, which runs approximately 4 km from north to south. Its width varies from 40 to 95 m. To the north, it leads to the 46 m Pyramid of the Moon. Following the armed attack on April 20, 2026, access to this pyramid was prohibited: admire it from the avenue and ask at the entrance whether the rule has changed. Allow a good hour for the walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Teotihuacán, Real del Monte, Tlaxcala, and Puebla in 7 Days

places.name: Tequisquiapan Que

visits.text: You’ll stroll through Miguel Hidalgo Square in Tequisquiapan, lined with cut-stone arcades. The village received the Pueblo Mágico designation in 2012. At its center, the parish church of Santa María de la Asunción has a neoclassical facade of pink stone. It was built in stages, and its dome was not completed until 1921. A monument in the village commemorates a decree by President Venustiano Carranza that made Tequisquiapan the country’s geographic center. On August 15, pre-Hispanic dances bring the square to life.

The Museo del Queso y el Vino is a good starting point for the wine and cheese route. Models, photographs, and screenings explain how both are made, followed by a tasting of products from the state. According to México Desconocido, the region is Mexico’s second-largest wine region, with more than 600 hectares of vineyards. In May, the Feria del Queso y Vino, a cheese and wine fair, brings music and performances to La Pila Park.

activities.text: After more than six years of making fresh cheeses under the Néole brand, the same company opened Cava Bocanegra in Fuentezuelas, near Tequisquiapan. It is an underground cellar where cheeses inspired by European recipes are aged. The guided tour explains cheese aging, the slow maturation that gives cheese its flavor and texture. Finish with a cheese board paired with wines or craft beers from Querétaro.

You’ll see opal being extracted and polished at the Mina de Ópalo de La Trinidad, about ten minutes from downtown Tequisquiapan. Opal is a stone with shifting colors. The tour shows both stages: extracting the rough stone, then polishing it. Schedule it for the morning of your last day, before driving back to Querétaro.

map_keywords: Museo del Queso y el Vino Tequisquiapan

places.name: Tihosuco Roo

visits.text: Almost entirely destroyed more than 170 years ago, Tihosuco’s church remains the pride of the village. Completed in 1839, it was stormed by Maya fighters at the start of the Caste War. This Maya uprising began in 1847 and lasted more than fifty years. Its surviving walls have become a symbol of resistance. Even today, most residents speak Yucatec Maya. Walk around the church before visiting the museum.

Tihosuco’s Caste War Museum, small but renovated in 2024, displays weapons, documents, and images of the conflict. The village is the birthplace of Jacinto Pat (1797–1849), one of the first leaders on the Maya side. A statue honors him here. Opening hours are not widely publicized, so it’s best to visit in the morning.

days_plan.itin_title: The Mexican Caribbean in 8 Days: Holbox, Bacalar, and Mahahual

map_keywords: Museo de la Guerra de Castas Tihosuco

visits.text: Avenida Revolución is Tijuana's historic spine - souvenir shops, artisan galleries, colorful facades. Stroll south to reach Plaza Santa Cecilia, the city's oldest square, where mariachis perform from late afternoon onward.

CECUT—Centro Cultural Tijuana—is the most important cultural institution in northwestern Mexico. Opened in 1982, it welcomes over 1.5 million visitors annually. Its spherical concrete IMAX dome earned it the popular nickname “La Bola”. Inside: the Museo de las Californias, a 995-seat auditorium, and El Cubo, a 1,500 m² international exhibition space. Spot it from the street—it's the giant sphere on Paseo de los Héroes, 2 km from the border.
Mercado El Popo is Tijuana's liveliest traditional market. Spices, artisanal cheeses, tropical fruits, medicinal herbs: this is where locals do their shopping. Allow 45 minutes to explore and snack.

activities.text: Tijuana has established itself in recent years as a Mexican street food capital. Calle Coahuila and the alleys around CECUT are home to the best eateries: birria tacos dipped in consommé, shrimp ceviche, seafood at the counter. Dine early—the best spots close at 9 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Baja California Road Trip in Mexico: From the Desert to the Sea of Cortez

visits.text: Tizimín doesn’t warrant a full day, but the city deserves a lunch stop. Nicknamed the “City of Kings,” it celebrates the Three Wise Men with a large fair every year from late December to mid-January. Visit the Church of the Three Kings, dedicated to those same Wise Men. Tizimín is also the leading cattle-raising area in the state of Yucatán, so take the opportunity to try some grilled meat.

days_plan.itin_title: The Mexican Caribbean in 8 Days: Holbox, Bacalar, and Mahahual

visits.text: The city’s best history lesson is painted on the walls: the murals in the Palacio de Gobierno de Tlaxcala cover more than 450 m². Painter Desiderio Hernández Xochitiotzin began them in 1957 with depictions of Tlaxcala before the Spanish arrived. He continued with the Conquest, then the following centuries, until his health forced him to stop in 2001. The palace houses state government offices, so enter quietly.

Orange walls and cobalt-blue talavera tiles: the Parroquia de San José brings color to central Tlaxcala. Talavera is hand-painted earthenware typical of the Puebla region. An earthquake destroyed the church’s dome and roof in 1864; those you see today date from the reconstruction. The Plaza de la Constitución, the central square laid out in 1524, measures 75 m on each side. Start your visit here: the entire center is walkable.

Tlaxcala’s monastery, built between 1537 and 1542, is among the first four Franciscan monasteries in the Americas. Its church, now the Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, retains its original roof structure of massive wooden beams. Its nave offers a rare example of Mudéjar art in the Americas, a style inherited from Spain’s Muslim artisans and characterized by geometric patterns. The cloister has housed the Museo Regional de Tlaxcala since 1981: allow 30 minutes for its collections.

From the outside, the Basílica de Ocotlán stands out for its earthenware tiles and red brick, typical of Tlaxcala’s Baroque architecture. Inside, the statue of the Virgin occupies a Baroque room covered in sculpted stucco, with eight twisted columns. Francisco Miguel Tlayoltehuanitzin created this decoration between 1715 and 1740. This is a pilgrimage site, so keep a low profile during Mass.

If you have 1 hour left, step into the Museo de Arte de Tlaxcala, which opened in 2004. The 19th-century building was first a hospital, then a prison, before becoming a museum. Six rooms display the permanent collection, and five host temporary exhibitions. Ask at the front desk which exhibition is currently on view.

Finish in Tizatlán at a 16th-century open chapel, meaning an outward-facing chapel from which Mass was celebrated before a crowd gathered outdoors. It was built on the platform of a pyramid that formed part of the palace of Xicohténcatl the Elder, a Tlaxcalan leader. Fragments of murals still depict the baptism of Christ and the Three Wise Men. Tizatlán is outside the historic center, so plan to drive.

days_plan.itin_title: Teotihuacán, Real del Monte, Tlaxcala, and Puebla in 7 Days

activities.text: Head up to the 44th floor of the Torre Latinoamericana at sunset, when the city lights come on. Completed in 1956, this 166 m tower survived the earthquakes of 1957 and 1985 without damage, while neighboring buildings were destroyed. Its secret lies in its steel frame and piles, long posts driven deep into the soft ground. The observation deck stays open until 9 p.m. on weekdays and 10 p.m. on weekends. Expect to pay about 170 pesos per adult.

days_plan.itin_title: Mexico City in 3 Days: Zócalo, Frida Kahlo, and Xochimilco

visits.text: The Cristo de las Noas measures 21.8 meters and was built between 1973 and 2000 with 580 tons of reinforced concrete. It dominates the Cerro de las Noas, visible from almost the entire city. The site includes replicas of five Holy Land chapels and an astronomical observatory.

Take the cable car from the centro histórico, on Avenida Treviño: 1,437 meters at 150 meters height to Puerto Noas. The arrival station at the top overlooks a cultural space with a permanent dinosaur exhibition and panoramic view of Torreón and the Comarca Lagunera.

activities.text: Torreonenses simply call it "Puerto Noas" and make it their Sunday balcony. After the cable car, stay on the platform to watch the sun descend over the Laguna desert. The site's aviary and astronomical observatory allow you to extend the visit into the evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeast Mexico: Monterrey, Desert & Mapimí, 14 days

visits.text: The Tulum archaeological site perches on a 12-meter cliff above the Caribbean—the only fortified Mayan city on the coast. Arrive at 8am sharp: from 8 to 10am, no lines, no tour buses, and El Castillo stands out against turquoise water. After 11am, it's packed. The temple served as a lighthouse to guide Mayan canoes through the coral reef.

Gran Cenote, 3 kilometers from downtown Tulum, is a classic semi-open Yucatán cenote: stalactites on the ceiling, water at 25°C, small black fish. Snorkeling masks are provided at the entrance. At dawn, light streams through the opening and lights up the water in an unreal shade of blue.

The site of Cobá, reached by car from Tulum, covers 80 km² in the jungle, with its structures connected by 50 white Mayan roads (sacbeob). Rent a bicycle at the entrance: it is 4 km to Nohoch Mul, the main pyramid, which is 42 meters high. It reopened for climbing in December 2025 with a new wooden stairway. The summit offers a 360° view over the canopy.
Cenote Dos Ojos, 20 km from Tulum, is actually two cenotes linked by a 60-meter underground tunnel. The system forms part of Sac Actun—350 km mapped. The water stays at 25–26°C all year round.

activities.text: Swim at the beach below the ruins—accessible only to ticket holders. The water is calm, cliff shadows provide shade until 10am. It's the most distinctive spot to take a dip in the Caribbean.
Sunset and dinner in Tulum town—Avenida Tulum is packed with taquerías, mezcal bars, and pizzerias. Much more affordable than the beachfront hotel zone, where prices skyrocket.

Snorkeling or diving at Cenote Dos Ojos—the Barbie Line route (515 meters, 6 meters deep) winds between stalactites and fossils. You'll need two flashlights. On-site operators provide equipment and guides for both circuits.
Bike ride along Cobá's trails between structures buried in vegetation. You might spot spider monkeys or coatis. Only 10% of the site has been excavated—the rest sleeps beneath the jungle.

Mexico Road Trip: From the Mayan Caribbean to Mexico City

visits.text: A Maya tale claims that a dwarf, the son of a witch, built the Pirámide del Adivino, Uxmal’s Pyramid of the Magician, in a single night. Its tiers follow an oval plan, whereas Maya pyramids usually have right angles. In fact, it was built in several stages: a newer pyramid covers an older one. Nearby, the Cuadrángulo de las Monjas consists of four palaces surrounding a courtyard. The Spanish saw it as a convent, hence its name, the Nunnery Quadrangle. Arrive in the early afternoon to allow 3 hours for your visit, and bring water.

The Palacio del Gobernador, or Governor’s Palace, is, in our view, the most beautiful building in Uxmal. Its style, known as Puuc, combines smooth lower walls with a frieze carved with masks of Chaac, the rain god. The region is dry: each palace had its own chultún, an underground cistern dug to store rainwater. Admission in 2026: 586 pesos for foreign visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Yucatán in 6 Days: Mérida, Uxmal, Izamal, and Celestún

visits.text: Valladolid is a colonial town midway between Cancún and Mérida—colorful facades, cobblestone streets, and an easy pace that contrasts sharply with the coastal tourist frenzy. Calzada de los Frailes is the most photographed street: rainbow-painted houses, string lights, and horse-drawn carriages. In the evening, locals gather around marquesita stands.

The Convent of San Bernardino de Siena (1552) was built directly on top of a sacred cenote—Sis-Ha—to symbolize Catholic dominance over Mayan places of worship. Every evening at 8pm, a video mapping show is projected on the convent walls. Free admission.

activities.text: Cenote Suytun, 15 minutes by car from downtown, is an underground cavern with a stone walkway extending toward the center of the basin. The name means 'stone of the center' in Mayan. At noon, a ray of light falls exactly on the platform—the effect is spectacular but so are the crowds. Arrive at 9am opening time to have the light to yourself.

Valladolid municipal market for lunch—panuchos, salbutes, and sopa de lima. Dishes are prepared right in front of you, vendors compete for your attention from the entrance. It's delicious, affordable, and the atmosphere is authentic Yucatán.

days_plan.itin_title: Mexico Road Trip: From the Mayan Caribbean to Mexico City

places.name: Valle de Guadalupe

visits.text: Valle de Guadalupe: 150 wineries tucked into a desert valley 90 minutes from Tijuana. The valley produces 90% of Mexican wine—grape varieties like Nebbiolo and Tempranillo grow in granitic soil that was once a seabed. Set out on the Ruta del Vino early in the morning: the morning fog clings between the vines and vanishes before 10 a.m.

Monte Xanic is one of the founding estates of the valley's wine movement. Established in the 1980s, it was among the first wineries to demonstrate the potential of Guadalupe's terroir internationally. The tasting room overlooks the vineyards—with views across the entire valley.
Finca la Carrodilla is a pioneering organic wine estate in the region. The rough-stone cellar and biodynamic vineyards make it a standout on the Ruta del Vino. Arrive at opening time to avoid groups.

activities.text: Dine at one of the chef-led restaurants on the wine estates. Fauna, on the Bruma estate, is the most sought-after address: Baja Med cuisine, wood-fired cooking and outdoor tables among the cacti. Booking is essential in high season.

visits.text: White sand dunes in the middle of Coahuila—no one expects it. The Dunas de Bilbao, 14 km from Viesca, stretch over about 10 km² and owe their origin to the ancient dried-up lagunas of Mayrán and Viesca. Their surface reflects the sun like a mirror. Entry: about 30 MXN per person.

activities.text: Sandboarding on the Dunas de Bilbao is more physical than it looks: climbing back up a fine-sand dune at 35°C demands endurance. Boards are rented on-site. Otherwise, walk barefoot to the big dune that locals call 'la haute' for the circular view of the desert.

visits.text: The canals of Xochimilco, whose name means “field of flowers” in Nahuatl, wind between chinampas, cultivated plots created about 1,000 years ago. Mud from the lake bottom was piled onto rafts of branches tied to trees. As these rafts sank, they gradually formed islets. They are called “floating gardens,” but the chinampas rest on the bottom. About 170 km of canals remain, listed by UNESCO in 1987. The Nuevo Nativitas boat landing is open daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. and has a craft market.

activities.text: If you’re in a group, a trajinera quickly becomes affordable: in Xochimilco, you pay per boat, not per person. These colorful boats, propelled with a pole by a boatman, carry up to 18 passengers. In 2026, expect to pay 700 to 800 pesos per hour for the entire boat. Buy at the boat landing’s official ticket booth and ignore touts on motorcycles or bicycles. Agree on the duration and price before boarding. Come in the morning, and keep cash handy for vendors who pass by in boats.

visits.text: Neither restored nor abandoned, Hacienda Yaxcopoil has been preserved as it was. This 17th-century estate grew henequén, an agave whose leaves yield plant fiber. In the engine room, a German diesel engine from 1913 powered the machines that extracted fiber from the leaves until 1984. The one-hour guided tour, in Spanish, costs 200 pesos; a booklet is available in English and German. The hacienda is closed on Sundays. Look for its double Moorish arch beside Route 261.

places.name: Zacatecas

visits.text: Zacatecas sits between two hills—Cerro del Grillo and Cerro de la Bufa—at 2,450 meters elevation. All its streets are built in pink cantera, the local volcanic stone. Its historic center has been UNESCO-listed since 1993. Take the cable car up on your first evening: the gondola crosses the city diagonally, 200 meters above the rooftops. Views over the cathedral, towers, and narrow alleys.

Zacatecas Cathedral, built between 1729 and 1752, is considered the masterpiece of Mexican Churrigueresque baroque—the most ornamental style there is. Its main façade is a wall of sculptures: angels, saints, vases, drapery in relief, all carved in pink cantera. Look for details on the top level—the arabesques interweave until not a square centimeter of stone remains bare.

The Mina El Edén was worked from 1586 to 1960. Indigenous slaves extracted silver, gold, copper, zinc here—up to five deaths per day from tuberculosis and silicosis combined. Today a small tourist train takes you into the lit galleries. The walls still show tools from the era. At the back, an underground lake. And in the evening, a nightclub has opened in the main chamber—probably the strangest dance club in Mexico.

Climb up to Cerro de la Bufa, the hill overlooking Zacatecas. At the summit: the Museo de la Toma de Zacatecas, dedicated to the June 1914 battle during which Pancho Villa seized the city by defeating Huerta's federal troops. This victory marked a turning point in the Mexican Revolution. In front of the museum, equestrian statues of Villa, Felipe Ángeles, and Pánfilo Natera. 360° views over the city.

The Museo Pedro Coronel is housed in a former 17th-century Jesuit college. The painter Pedro Coronel, from Zacatecas, bequeathed his personal collection here: works by Picasso, Miró, Chagall, pre-Columbian masks, African and Oceanic pieces. It's one of Mexico's best-endowed provincial museums.

activities.text: First evening in Zacatecas: wander down Avenida Hidalgo, the city center's main artery, and settle into a restaurant on Plaza de Armas. Callejoneadas—nighttime strolls through the alleys with tamborazo brass bands—often depart from the plaza in late evening. A group of musicians with kettledrums and brass, a donkey loaded with mezcal, and everyone follows.

Evening callejoneada with tamborazo—the real deal. Tamborazo zacatecano is a 19th-century tradition born in the mines: miners who returned Saturday night with their pay and paraded through the alleys with brass bands until dawn. Join a group departing from Plaza de Armas and follow the procession through lantern-lit alleys.

visits.text: Mexico City residents call their large central square, the Plaza de la Constitución, “el Zócalo,” meaning “the pedestal.” A monument to independence was supposed to stand here. Only its pedestal was built and later buried, but the nickname stuck. The square measures about 240 m on each side, covering an area equivalent to eight soccer fields. Every day, a giant flag is raised and lowered here in a ceremony. Stay around the square and to the west: France Diplomatie advises against visiting neighborhoods to the north and northeast, such as Tepito and La Lagunilla.
